# Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents

Yingzhao Jian    Zhongan Wang    Yuxuan Hou & HeheFan\*
Affiliation: College of Artificial Intelligence, Zhejiang University.
\*Corresponding author. Email: [hehefan@zju.edu.cn](mailto:)

###### Abstract

Video director agents orchestrate multistage production to realize
users’ creative visions. Emerging research on their self-evolution
advances screenplay planning effectively. However, the mutual
reinforcement between directing and user interaction remains largely
overlooked. Improved interaction clarifies user intent and informs
workflow refinement, while more reliable execution shifts collaboration
from troubleshooting to creative decisions. To this end, we introduce
LIT (Learning to Interact and DirecT), a framework comprises a director
agent, a simulated user, and a meta engineer. Simulated user assigns
creative tasks to probe the director’s weaknesses, while the meta
engineer uses the task traces to revise the director’s interaction and
production strategy. Although this approach can address discovered
interaction and production issues, it still relies on passive
attribution by the meta agent. This limits its ability to adapt to
broader user interaction patterns and production techniques. To solve
this problem, we equip LIT with a co-evolution paradigm. The meta agent
proactively learns external knowledge, thereby improving its ability to
discover problems and propose solutions. The meta agent, simulated user,
and director together form an evolutionary closed loop, collaboratively
enhances the system’s directing and interaction capabilities. Across the
Test and OOD Test splits, LIT improves production and Interaction scores
by 19.1% and 32.0%, respectively, relative to the initial pipeline.
Controlled ablations reveal the correlation between improvements in
production and interaction, where the co-evolution mechanism further
encourage directing skill and interaction mode exploration.

## 1 Introduction

![Refer to caption](2610.41865v1/fig1_teaser.png)

Figure 1: Overview of LIT. (a) User interaction provides inspiration for
improving the director’s workflow. Feedback about a change in a
character’s face leads the director to create an actor card before
generation. (b) The meta engineer and the agent system co-evolve through
simulated user interactions. The meta engineer revises the director and
simulated user. It also updates its own evaluation criteria and revision
strategy. (c) The radar chart compares LIT with existing methods on
visual and audio consistency, motion, plot, interaction, and intent
fulfillment. (d) After evolution, the director asks for clarification
and feedback on drafts. The example also shows more consistent
characters and scenes.

AI video directors broaden access to cinematic storytelling, enabling
people to bring imagined worlds and narratives to the screen. They
translate creative intent into coordinated decisions across
scriptwriting, shot design, generation, and editing ([Xu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib1)). To improve this orchestration beyond individual
projects, recent research has begun to explore production-centered
self-evolution. These approaches refine reusable skills, workflow
configurations, and production policies from execution feedback,
allowing lessons from earlier videos to improve subsequent planning and
generation ([Wei et al., 2026](#bib.bib2); [Liu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib3)).

The user determines what a successful video should express, yet an
initial request rarely captures every choice that shapes that
expression. Directing therefore requires interaction: clarifying
creative priorities, recognizing delegated decisions, and negotiating
revisions as drafts emerge. User-guided creation supports this process
through dialogue and feedback, which can also inform workflow
refinement ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib5); [Wang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib4)). However, these approaches primarily use interaction
to guide production. The interaction strategy itself is seldom treated
as an evolving counterpart to the production workflow. This leaves their
reciprocal improvement across projects largely unexplored. Poorly timed
feedback can force revisions across completed assets and shots, while
unreliable execution keeps users occupied with troubleshooting instead
of creative decisions.

Our insight is that interaction and production are mutually reinforcing
targets of evolution. Interaction reveals intent and workflow
limitations that execution feedback alone may miss. Reliable production
enables users to provide more informed creative feedback. In
Fig. [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents")(a),
the user points out that a character’s face has changed. This feedback
motivates a reusable workflow change: create an actor card before
generation to maintain character consistency.
Fig. [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents")(d)
illustrates the joint improvement in production and interaction after
evolution. The director clarifies scene preferences and requests
feedback on drafts, while producing more consistent characters and
scenes. Together, these examples illustrate our goal of improving both
the production workflow and the interaction strategy across projects.

To this end, we introduce LIT (Learning to Interact and DirecT), a
self-improving video creation framework comprising a director agent, a
simulated user, and a meta engineer. When an evolution task begins, the
simulated user first assigns a creative task to the director. This task
is generated according to a user persona, and is designed to expose
defects in the director’s interaction and production strategies. The
director then receives the request and elicits further intent through
dialogue and draft reviews. During this process, the simulated user may
clarify preferences, delegate routine choices, or request revisions.
Finally, the meta engineer analyzes the resulting dialogue and
production traces, thereby revising the director’s interaction strategy
and directing workflow. These revisions persist across projects,
allowing each interaction to inform how future videos are made.

Although this process can solve problems exposed through outcome
evaluation and defect attribution, it still depends largely on the meta
engineer’s ability to discover problems and explore solutions. Existing
methods, however, rely on a fixed meta-engineer design, whose capacity
for defect localization remains static and thus limits problem coverage.
To address this, we equip LIT with a curiosity-driven co-evolution
mechanism. During evolution, the meta engineer proactively learns
external knowledge, improving its ability to discover problems and
propose solutions. The meta engineer, the simulated user, and the
director together form an evolutionary closed loop that collaboratively
enhances the system’s directing and interaction capabilities.

We evaluate LIT on held-out video creation tasks and user profiles.
Across the Test and OOD Test splits, LIT improves production and
Interaction scores by 19.1% and 32.0%, respectively, relative to the
initial pipeline. These gains use a 2:1 weighting of the two splits to
match their sample counts. In a user study, participants prefer LIT for
intent fulfillment in 51.7% of group assessments (31 of 60), compared
with ViMax and VideoWeaver. Controlled ablations show that production
and interaction learning reinforce each other, while Co-evolution
further enhances this process.

In summary, our contributions are threefold:

- •
  We identify interaction and production are mutually reinforcing during
  director evolution.
- •
  We propose a co-evolution mechanism that evolves the meta engineer
  itself through proactive external knowledge learning, enhancing its
  ability to improve both production and interaction.
- •
  LIT improves production and Interaction scores by 19.1% and 32.0%,
  respectively, relative to the initial pipeline across the Test and OOD
  Test splits.

Figure 2: LIT learns from user interaction and video production across
epochs. Left: The director asks the simulated user to clarify intent and
uses the answers to guide production. Center: The meta engineer analyzes
videos and production traces to identify problems. It uses memory and
external references to propose skill and evaluation updates. It also
schedules validation and designs tasks to expose weaknesses and test new
methods. Right: Accepted revisions guide the meta engineer, simulated
user, and director in the next epoch.

## 2 Method

LIT is a harness framework for co-evolution between a meta engineer and
an agent system across video creation projects, aimed at improving both
directing and user interaction. In each project, a video director
collaborates with a simulated user to construct and execute a production
pipeline. A meta engineer analyzes the resulting dialogue, execution
traces, and artifacts to refine the director’s production workflow and
interaction strategies. It learns from successful and failed revisions
to update its own task selection and revision strategies. An overview of
the co-creation and co-evolution process is shown in
Fig. [2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents").

To support evolution and assess its outcomes, we construct a dataset
pairing scripts with user personas. Each pair provides the simulated
user with the creative context and behavioral guidance for its
interactions with the director.

### 2.1 Director-User Interaction Dataset

We construct a director–user interaction dataset by pairing video
directing tasks wit user persona. Specifically, we extract directing
task from video and plot dataset, and leverage LLM for persona
synthesis. Each persona specifies the user’s production knowledge,
communication style, and disclosure behavior, shaping both the initial
request and subsequent responses. During persona-consistent
verification, clarification and adversarial probes test these responses,
and reviewer feedback guides revisions to the persona and disclosure
policy
(Fig. [3](#S2.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 2.1 Director-User Interaction Dataset ‣ 2 Method ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents")).

##### Example case.

Consider the following illustrative exchange about the lighting of an
interior scene.

Director: “What kind of lighting would you like in the room?”

- •
  User A (professional persona): “Use low-key lighting, with a soft side
  key and a subtle cool rim light.”
- •
  User B (non-professional persona): “I’m not sure about lighting. Could
  you show me a few examples so I can choose?”

The first response specifies an actionable lighting setup. the second
requests visual alternatives, requiring the director to help the user
articulate a preference.

The dataset contains 240 tasks, 284 reference-material entries, and 892
planned shots.
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Dataset Construction ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents")
provides further details on construction, task distributions, and
persona settings.

### 2.2 Simulated Director–User Interaction

LIT uses a skill-driven harness in which evolvable skills govern most of
the control flow, agent coordination, and evolution procedures. These
structures can be revised together with the agents’ production,
interaction, and evolution strategies.

At evolution epoch $`k`$, we denote the editable resource bundles of the
director, simulated user, and meta engineer by $`D_{k}`$, $`U_{k}`$, and
$`M_{k}`$, respectively. Each bundle contains governing skills,
supporting tools, and assets. A shared runtime $`\mathcal{F}`$ (e.g.,
Codex, Claude Code, or OpenClaw) instantiates the meta engineer
$`m_{k}`$, simulated user $`u_{k,i}`$, and director $`d_{k}`$ as:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
m_{k}=\mathcal{F}[M_{k}],\quad\{(s_{i},p_{i})\}_{i=1}^{B}\leftarrow m_{k}(\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{evo}},\mathcal{H}_{k}),\quad u_{k,i}=\mathcal{F}[U_{k};s_{i},p_{i}],\quad d_{k}=\mathcal{F}[D_{k}],
``` |  | (1) |

where the meta engineer writes a script $`s_{i}`$ and persona $`p_{i}`$
for a simulated user, drawing on the evolution dataset
$`\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{evo}}`$. $`\mathcal{H}_{k}`$ is the evolution
history, $`i`$ is the project index, and $`B`$ is the number of projects
in a batch. For clarity, we suppress the epoch index on project-specific
quantities and omit the agents’ execution contexts.

For each project, the user first provides an initial production prompt
$`t_{i}`$ to the director. The director then develops and executes a
production plan specifying the workflow and the skills required at each
stage. During production, it may query the user about narrative or
design details, receiving a response $`a_{i,j}=u_{i}(q_{i,j})`$ to its
$`j`$-th question. These responses inform revisions to the plan or
intermediate artifacts. The complete interaction is expressed as:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
(v_{i},h_{d,i},h_{u,i})\leftarrow d_{k}(u_{i}),\qquad h_{u,i}=\bigl(t_{i},(q_{i,j},a_{i,j})_{j=1}^{J_{i}}\bigr),
``` |  | (2) |

where $`h_{d,i}`$ and $`h_{u,i}`$ denote the production trajectory and
interaction history, respectively, and $`J_{i}`$ is the number of
question–answer exchanges.

After each batch, the meta engineer analyzes the generated videos,
production trajectories, and interaction histories to revise the role
bundles, thereby closing the evolution loop:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
(D_{k+1},U_{k+1},M_{k+1})\leftarrow m_{k}\left(\{(v_{i},h_{d,i},h_{u,i})\}_{i=1}^{B},\mathcal{H}_{k}\right).
``` |  | (3) |

### 2.3 Meta Engineer Co-evolution

The evolution procedure follows a hypothetico-deductive paradigm, which
largely depends on problem discovery and solution exploration. However,
existing methods rely on fixed self-improvement harness designs. The
meta engineer’s criteria and capacity for defect localization remain
static, limiting the problem coverage. In addition, revision relies on
reactive defect attribution, which constrains solution diversity.

Motivated by these observations, we introduce a curiosity-driven
co-evolution harness for director–user interaction. The meta engineer
proactively evolves its evaluation criteria and development capabilities
through web data mining and reflection. The user assigns creation
projects that expose defects, while encouraging the director to explore
novel skills. In this process, a curriculum-learning schedule balances
exploration and optimization, collaboratively raising the ceiling of
evolution.

Proactive reflection and exploration. After each revision, the meta
engineer first reflects on historical evolution trajectories. It then
searches the web for AI videos, audience comments, and technical
analyses. By comparing these materials with previous iterations, it
identifies under-explored topics and evaluation criteria, and uncovers
potential solutions and alternatives. The meta engineer also proactively
verifies individual production steps or its own evaluation criteria,
thereby discovering improvements beyond reactive attribution.

User-driven evolution scheduling. We incorporate curriculum learning
along the evolution process. Based on pipeline maturity and historical
evaluation results, the meta engineer designs interaction tasks with
different difficulty levels and categories for the current evolution
epoch. The user carries out the interaction tasks, which elicit defect
exposure through targeted plot design, and encourage the trial of novel
directing skills. Finally, the meta engineer proposes revision plans
accordingly, drawing on its evolving solution library as a reference.

## 3 Experiments

### 3.1 Experimental Setup

We evaluate LIT’s evolution trajectory and video directing performance
on the constructed dataset. For the trajectory, we reports both the
evaluation results and process metrics after each epoch, thereby
analyzing the correlation between user interaction and production
capabilities.

Regarding directing performance, we compare with existing
state-of-the-art video directing agents, including fixed and
self-evolving variants. We further test the impact of each component,
and verify the generalization across different base models. Finally, we
conduct human evaluations and examine the alignment between machine and
human judgments.

At test time, each compared method interacts with the privileged User
described in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Evaluation Protocol ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents").
This User has access to the complete task specification and persona. The
Director receives only the public request and information disclosed
through the conversation according to the User’s disclosure rules.

#### 3.1.1 Metrics

We evaluate generated videos along six aspects related to directing and
user interaction. Specifically, we evaluate visual, audio, motion, plot,
interaction, and intent. These aspects fall under four higher-level
dimensions: Consistency (visual, audio), Dynamic (motion, plot),
Interaction, and Intent. Each aspect is graded by an LLM against a
predefined checklist. Details can be found in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Evaluation Protocol ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents").

For user preference analysis, we compute Kendall’s $`\tau`$ between user
and evaluator rankings. Overall, Consistency is assessed through Visual
and Audio, Dynamic through Motion and Plot, while Interaction and Intent
are each assessed directly.

#### 3.1.2 Implementation

We implement LIT based on Codex skills. We use Qwen3.8-27B model with
W8A8 quantization. The reasoning effort is set to low, with a context
length of 262K, and auto-compact at 220K. Video generation uses
Minimax-H3 through ComfyUI, with 4-step turbo inference LoRA. Music is
generated by MiniMax-Music3. Sound effects are generated by Woosh. Vocal
separation uses Mel-RoFormer. All the above models are locally deployed
on Ascend 910C NPU servers.

Image generation, ASR, audio understanding, TTS, and embedding and
reranking are provided by commercial cloud APIs, specifically
Nano-Banana-2-Lite, Qwen-Audio-3.0-ASR-Flash, Qwen3.5-Omni-Plus,
Qwen3-TTS-Instruct-Flash, Qwen3-Embedding, and Qwen3-Rerank.

For evaluation, we uses 4 agent voting with Qwen3.8-27B xhigh reasoning
effort. The multimodal perception suite for evaluation is consistent
with the above. For the ground-truth samples in OOD-test, we use videos
manually crafted with the same toolchain. Each handcrafted video is
reviewed to ensure quality.

### 3.2 Comparison between Video Director Agents

##### Setting.

We compare LIT with state-of-the-art video directing and self-evolution
methods. Within them, ViMax and
VideoClaw^([2](#footnote2 "footnote 2 ‣ Table 1 ‣ 2.3 Meta Engineer Co-evolution ‣ 2 Method ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents"))
are the latest directing pipeline. GenMAC and VideoWeaver performs
in-project and cross-project evolution, respectively. We additionally
included general-purpose methods, including
GPT-6-Astra^([1](#footnote1 "footnote 1 ‣ Table 1 ‣ 2.3 Meta Engineer Co-evolution ‣ 2 Method ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents"))
and GEPA.

The evolution experiments use four epochs on the same task collection
and infrastructure. Development, validation, and production budgets
differ across methods. The comparison therefore measures performance
under the method-specific budgets described in
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Comparison Methods ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents").
We report automatic and human evaluation results. Finally, we provide
visualization of generated videos for qualitative assessment.

Quantitative Results. As shown in
Tab. [1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 2.3 Meta Engineer Co-evolution ‣ 2 Method ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents"),
LIT achieves average scores of 85.7 and 76.4, respectively. On the
interaction dimensions, LIT exceeds existing methods by 9.2%
(Interaction) and 6.7% (Intent) on average, with the Test Split weighted
2 and the OOD Test weighted 1. These results demonstrate the
effectiveness of a self-improving user interaction strategy.

For the gains summarized in the abstract and introduction, we use Before
Evo. in
Tab. [1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 2.3 Meta Engineer Co-evolution ‣ 2 Method ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents")
as the baseline. Production is the mean of Visual, Audio, Motion, and
Plot scores. We aggregate each score across the 32 Test and 16 OOD Test
cases with weights of 2:1, then compute its relative increase over the
baseline. Production rises from 68.38 to 81.48, a 19.1% relative
increase. Interaction rises from 67.13 to 88.59, a 32.0% relative
increase.

As shown in
Tab. [1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 2.3 Meta Engineer Co-evolution ‣ 2 Method ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents"),
LIT improves the pipeline by 17.9% and 30.1% on the Test and OOD-test
Split, respectively. VideoWeaver, GenMAC, and GEPA improve by 7.8/19.7%,
3.8/10.6%, and 1.7/9.7%, respectively. GEPA validate every modification
by a full rollout of the pipeline, which leaves little budget for
evolution in such a costly video generation setting. GenMAC evolves
within a single project and lacks cross-project experience, whereas
VideoWeaver keeps the meta agent fixed during evolution. In contrast,
LIT explicitly models the user and co-evolves the interaction policy
with the production workflow, enabling the learned capabilities to
generalize across projects.

##### Qualitative Results.

ViMax exhibits actor duplication and inconsistent props, which are
common problems for director agents without targeted revision. GenMAC
performs self-improvement on a single project, but within a single
project, it is difficult to discover and resolve scene consistency
issues. VideoWeaver achieves scene consistency through cross-project
attribution, but due to evaluation limitations, it does not learn
character blocking consistency. LIT’s co-evolution mechanism effectively
improves the meta agent’s problem discovery and resolution capabilities,
achieving high-quality video direction
(Figs. [4](#S3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Qualitative Results. ‣ 3.2 Comparison between Video Director Agents ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents")
and [6](#S3.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 3.4 Ablation Study ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents")).

![Refer to caption](2610.41865v1/fig_visualization.png)

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison on the same plot. Baselines show

character count and positioning. LIT shows better visual continuity in

##### User Study.

We conduct a user study with $`15`$ participants. Each method generates
16 videos. For each participant, we randomly sample 4 pairs of videos
generated by different methods in a blind and randomized order, and the
participant selects the preferred one along the corresponding evaluation
dimension. We report the number of wins under user evaluation and
machine evaluation, respectively. We further compute Kendall’s $`\tau`$
between human preferences and automatic metrics to validate the
rationality of our evaluation metrics.

As shown in
Tab. [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ User Study. ‣ 3.2 Comparison between Video Director Agents ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents"),
LIT achieves the most user preferences. The machine evaluation metrics
achieve an average Kendall’s $`\tau`$ of 0.833 with human preferences,
demonstrating a strong correlation.

### 3.3 Evolution Process of User-Director Interaction

##### Evolution Curve.

We run the evolution process for four rounds
(Fig. [5](#S3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ User Study. ‣ 3.2 Comparison between Video Director Agents ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents")).
Each round we measure the interaction and production capabilities of the
director agent. Both capabilities are evaluated on the held-out and OOD
test set. To analyze their collaborative improvement effect, we further
conduct ablation studies, in which the production workflow and the
interaction policy are frozen, respectively. We compare these ablation
curves with those under joint evolution.

The results in
Fig. [5](#S3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ User Study. ‣ 3.2 Comparison between Video Director Agents ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents")(a)
and (b) show a joint improvement in Interaction and Production
capabilities, with their evolution effects mutually reinforcing each
other. User Interaction raises the capability upper bound of Production.
The lack of Production evolution limits the ability to fulfill User
Intent, which leads to degraded performance in Interaction.

##### Process-Oriented Results.

Due to the multi-step nature of the directing workflow, the agent’s
actual improvements at certain steps may not necessarily be reflected in
the final evaluation results. Therefore, we analyzed LIT’s process
metrics to provide a more comprehensive perspective. Specifically, we
evaluated technical maturity, user interaction modes, and changes in
meta criteria.

Technical maturity is evaluated using a predefined checklist of common
directing practices extracted from open-source, handcrafted workflows.
User interaction modes are divided into three categories: requesting
clarification, requesting review, and providing ideas. These categories
reflect changes in the agent’s mode of collaboration with the user. We
also analyze changes in the meta engineer’s evaluation criteria, which
guides the evolution of the director.

As shown in
Fig. [5](#S3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ User Study. ‣ 3.2 Comparison between Video Director Agents ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents")(c),
the curve of Technical maturity exhibits consistent growth and is more
stable than the trend of production quality. The changes in Evaluation
Criteria are as follows:

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The results indicate that the model’s evolutionary focus shifts from
fixing obvious defects to optimizing details. Moreover, based on the
number and distribution of issues in
Fig. [5](#S3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ User Study. ‣ 3.2 Comparison between Video Director Agents ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents")(d),
the model becomes more proactive in user interaction, evolving from
initially requesting information to providing production ideas.

### 3.4 Ablation Study

We compare the performance of LIT on various VLM backbones, and conduct
ablations on different components of our framework. Due to cost
constraints, each epoch generates eight videos. On top of the evolved
framework, we additionally tried 20-step inference to examine the impact
of the video foundation model.

Based on the results in
Tab. [3](#S3.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 3.4 Ablation Study ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents"),
LIT is effective across multiple VLM backbones. Models with stronger
multimodal capabilities have stronger directing capabilities, but they
also introduce more retries, leading to higher costs. 20-step inference
improved Dynamic performance, indicating that video dynamics are
strongly correlated with the foundation model.

Ablation studies show that the improvement of Interaction and Production
capabilities has a synergistic effect, validating the effectiveness of
LIT’s explicit modeling of users. Co-Evo effectively improves the
model’s performance by exploring defects and solution proactively, while
keeping costs controllable.

##### User Study.

We conduct a user study with $`15`$ participants. Each method generates
16 videos. For each participant, we randomly sample 4 pairs of videos
generated by different methods in a blind and randomized order, and the
participant selects the preferred one along the corresponding evaluation
dimension. We report the number of wins under user evaluation and
machine evaluation, respectively. We further compute Kendall’s $`\tau`$
between human preferences and automatic metrics to validate the
rationality of our evaluation metrics.

As shown in
Tab. [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ User Study. ‣ 3.2 Comparison between Video Director Agents ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents"),
LIT achieves the most user preferences. The machine evaluation metrics
achieve an average Kendall’s $`\tau`$ of 0.833 with human preferences,
demonstrating a strong correlation.

## 4 Conclusion

We presented LIT, a framework that jointly evolves the interaction
strategies and production workflows of AI video directors. Through
persona-grounded creative tasks, simulated user dialogue, draft
feedback, and execution traces, LIT converts project-level experience
into reusable improvements: the director learns to elicit latent
creative intent and coordinate more reliable production, while the meta
engineer diagnoses and revises both aspects of its behavior. Crucially,
LIT introduces curiosity-driven co-evolution, enabling the meta engineer
to proactively acquire external knowledge and refine its own evaluation
criteria and revision strategies. This expands its ability to discover
and resolve previously uncovered interaction and production failures,
rather than relying on a fixed capacity for evolution. Experiments on
held-out Test and OOD Test tasks show improvements of 19.1% in
production and 32.0% in interaction over the initial pipeline, while
user studies further demonstrate stronger intent fulfillment. Ablation
studies confirm that interaction and production learning are mutually
reinforcing and that co-evolution provides additional gains. Overall,
LIT suggests that video directors can improve across projects not only
by learning how to produce better videos, but also by learning how to
collaborate with users and how to improve the process by which they
evolve.

## Appendix A Supplementary Related Work

### A.1 AI Video Directors

AI video directors translate users’ creative intent into videos through
structured scene planning ([Lin et al., 2024](#bib.bib6); [Long et al.,
2024](#bib.bib12)) and role-based production coordination ([Xu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib1); [Wu et al., 2025](#bib.bib7); [Shi et al.,
2025](#bib.bib13)). Recent human-guided systems support stage-specific
review ([Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib4)) and creator-driven
refinement ([Savytski et al., 2026](#bib.bib8)), but rely on predefined
interaction protocols. LIT makes these protocols learnable, evolving
interaction policies that adapt to user preferences and improve with
experience across projects.

### A.2 Director Agent Self-Evolution

Self-evolution aims to help video directors better realize users’
creative visions. Existing methods pursue this goal through prompt and
layout refinement ([Huang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib9); [Long et al.,
2025](#bib.bib10)) or creative configuration search ([Song et al.,
2026](#bib.bib11)). Others improve workflow instructions ([Wang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib5)), orchestration skills ([Wei et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)),
or stage-specific policies ([Liu et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)) across
projects. However, these efforts evolve production while overlooking
user interaction. LIT explicitly models users, thereby driving the
mutual improvement of directing and user intent alignment.

### A.3 LLM Agent v.s. Workflow

Figure 7: Workflow and agent control in video production. Top: A
framework executes six production stages in a predefined sequence.
Bottom: An agent accesses the same stages as independent capabilities,
selecting its next action according to context and feedback. The shared
connector indicates access, not execution order.

An agent is an LLM-based system in which the model decides how to
proceed and which tools to invoke. A workflow is a system that
coordinates LLM calls and tools through code-defined execution
paths ([Anthropic, 2024](#bib.bib18)). Their difference lies in control:
agents determine the course of execution at runtime, whereas workflows
prescribe its structure
(Fig. [7](#A1.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ A.3 LLM Agent v.s. Workflow ‣ Appendix A Supplementary Related Work ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents")).
LIT is a video-director agent with an evolving workflow-skill harness,
combining agent flexibility with the procedural guidance of a workflow.

##### Agent.

Early tool-augmented agents established model-directed access to
external information and actions ([Yao et al., 2023](#bib.bib23);
[Schick et al., 2023](#bib.bib39)). Execution feedback then became a
source of reusable knowledge, enabling agents to carry lessons beyond
the current reasoning trace ([Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib24); [Wang et
al., 2023](#bib.bib15); [Zhao et al., 2024](#bib.bib40)). This shift
from isolated tool calls to sustained execution also motivates
general-purpose runtimes. Claude Code³³ 3
[https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code)
and Codex⁴⁴ 4
[https://github.com/openai/codex](https://github.com/openai/codex) place
model-directed action within a persistent working
environment ([Anthropic, 2025](#bib.bib19); [OpenAI, 2026](#bib.bib20)).
This autonomy also introduces execution variability, making procedural
guidance important for long-running tasks ([Anthropic,
2024](#bib.bib18); [Wei et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)).

Video agents constrain long-horizon decisions through specialized
production roles ([Xu et al., 2025](#bib.bib1); [Wu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib7)). Search and refinement further address unreliable
individual generations ([Shi et al., 2025](#bib.bib13); [Song et al.,
2026](#bib.bib11)). However, unconstrained agent execution can be
unstable: locally plausible decisions may produce an inconsistent
production process ([Anthropic, 2024](#bib.bib18); [Wei et al.,
2026](#bib.bib2)). LIT encodes production workflows as skills that guide
the director’s execution. These skills preserve procedural structure and
accumulate improvements across projects, providing workflow-based
constraints on autonomous decisions.

##### Workflow.

Workflow development has moved from explicit orchestration toward
automated design. Component and graph frameworks expose the execution
structure for composition, as in LangChain⁵⁵ 5
[https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain)
and LangGraph⁶⁶ 6
[https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph) ([LangChain,
2026a](#bib.bib21); [LangChain, 2026b](#bib.bib22)). With this structure
specified, program-level optimization can revise component instructions
using downstream feedback ([Khattab et al., 2024](#bib.bib25);
[Yuksekgonul et al., 2024](#bib.bib42); [Agrawal et al.,
2026](#bib.bib45)). A broader search space also admits changes to the
computation itself, which reduces dependence on a manually chosen agent
or workflow architecture ([Hu et al., 2025](#bib.bib26); [Zhang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib27)). The underlying trade-off is between predictable
execution and adaptation to tasks that depart from the prescribed
process ([Anthropic, 2024](#bib.bib18)).

In video production, explicit plans coordinate separate generation
stages ([Lin et al., 2024](#bib.bib6); [Long et al., 2024](#bib.bib12)).
Evolving workflows and reusable skills allow production experience to
improve that sequence ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib5); [Wei et al.,
2026](#bib.bib2); [Liu et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)). However, a fixed
execution structure remains rigid when a project requires a different
production path. Improving instructions within that structure alone does
not give the system discretion to reorganize it. LIT represents workflow
guidance as revisable skills within an agent architecture. The director
adapts their application to the current project, while skill evolution
retains accumulated production expertise. This combines flexible
execution with progressively refined workflow guidance.

### A.4 User Intent Understanding of LLM Agents

Intent understanding involves acquiring enough information to act and
maintaining agreement during execution. Conversational tool-use
benchmarks connect dialogue to observable task outcomes, extending from
agent-controlled execution to shared user–agent control ([Yao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib28); [Barres et al., 2025](#bib.bib29)). Within this
setting, clarification is a decision problem: an unanswered question
matters when it changes the appropriate action. SAGE-Agent formalizes
this connection through uncertainty over tool arguments and the expected
value of clarification ([Suri et al., 2026](#bib.bib30)).

In creative production, feedback on intermediate artifacts helps make an
underspecified intention actionable. AnimAgents organizes that feedback
across pre-production stages ([Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib4)). CHIEF
extends the loop to generated videos, combining creator revisions with
audience-conditioned critique ([Savytski et al., 2026](#bib.bib8)). User
feedback alone cannot correct an interaction policy that fails to elicit
useful creative direction. Users may struggle to articulate preferences,
while poorly realized previews make those preferences harder to judge.
LIT jointly improves interaction and production through simulated
collaborations. Dialogue reveals where guidance is ineffective, and
production outcomes reveal whether the elicited intent was actionable.
The resulting updates connect better creative communication to more
faithful execution.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### A.5 Long Video Generation and Evaluation

Long-video generation requires coherence beyond a local generation
window. A short clip, such as a 15-second segment, may depict a single
event. A longer production must preserve story state across successive
events and shot transitions. Duration extension and multi-shot
storytelling therefore pose related but distinct problems ([Kim et al.,
2024](#bib.bib35); [Kara et al., 2025](#bib.bib36)). In agent-directed
production, the relevant horizon also includes decisions made before
rendering, whose consequences can persist throughout the film ([Wu et
al., 2025](#bib.bib7); [Liu et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)).

#### A.5.1 Long Video Generation

Two main approaches address this extended horizon: model-level temporal
generation and production-level orchestration. FIFO-Diffusion extends
pretrained generators through queued denoising, while ShotAdapter
introduces shot-specific conditioning within a diffusion model ([Kim et
al., 2024](#bib.bib35); [Kara et al., 2025](#bib.bib36)). The
orchestration approach instead decomposes a story into controllable
generation tasks. VideoDirectorGPT establishes an LLM-guided planning
scheme, and VideoStudio uses shared entity information for consistent
multi-scene synthesis ([Lin et al., 2024](#bib.bib6); [Long et al.,
2024](#bib.bib12)). These methods connect local synthesis to
longer-range visual structure.

MovieAgent coordinates production through hierarchical planning ([Wu et
al., 2025](#bib.bib7)). AniMaker and Co-Director use search to refine
generation decisions ([Shi et al., 2025](#bib.bib13); [Song et al.,
2026](#bib.bib11)). CHIEF incorporates creator feedback into video
refinement ([Savytski et al., 2026](#bib.bib8)), while
production-evolution methods retain improvements across projects ([Wei
et al., 2026](#bib.bib2); [Liu et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)). Visual
continuity does not ensure fidelity to the intended story. A mistaken
interpretation established during planning can persist across an
otherwise coherent sequence. Production-only optimization leaves the
interaction that produced this interpretation uncorrected. LIT uses
dialogue alongside production traces to revise both intent understanding
and its realization throughout the workflow.

Tab. [4](#A1.T4 "Table 4 ‣ A.5.1 Long Video Generation ‣ A.5 Long Video Generation and Evaluation ‣ Appendix A Supplementary Related Work ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents")
distinguishes generation capabilities from the mechanisms used to
improve them. User interaction concerns collaboration during creation.
Meta co-evolution concerns joint improvement of the production system
and its meta-level optimizer. Defect attribution includes critic-based
identification of the production stage responsible for an error.

#### A.5.2 Long Video Evaluation

Video evaluation has expanded from perceptual quality to the realization
of structured events. VBench measures distinct dimensions of visual
quality and consistency, while VBench-2.0 adds tests of physical and
semantic faithfulness ([Huang et al., 2024](#bib.bib37); [Zheng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib38)). At the production level, FilmBench evaluates
cinematic control, and CineScope measures episode-level narrative and
directorial coherence ([Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib16); [Liu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib3)). VideoWeaver further uses execution traces to assess
the generation process ([Wei et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)). This progression
provides evidence about both the completed film and the procedure that
produced it.

Conversational benchmarks assess task outcomes together with user–agent
coordination ([Yao et al., 2024](#bib.bib28); [Barres et al.,
2025](#bib.bib29)). In video production, judging against the disclosed
prompt cannot reveal requirements that the director failed to elicit.
Output and execution scores alone also leave the source of creative
misalignment ambiguous. LIT evaluates the completed film against a
private creative specification and examines the dialogue that informed
production. This distinguishes a requirement that was never elicited
from one that was understood but poorly executed. The distinction
supports targeted improvement of the interaction policy or production
workflow while keeping final-video quality independently measurable.

### A.6 LLM Agent Self-evolution

Agent self-evolution has expanded from retaining experience to revising
the system that uses it. Early approaches preserve feedback as external
knowledge, improving later decisions without changing model
weights ([Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib24); [Wang et al.,
2023](#bib.bib15); [Zhao et al., 2024](#bib.bib40)). Subsequent work
treats the agent program as an optimization variable, allowing execution
evidence to change its instructions or structure ([Agrawal et al.,
2026](#bib.bib45); [Hu et al., 2025](#bib.bib26); [Zhang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib14)). A further direction adapts the learning conditions
themselves through coupled curricula or an evolving improvement
procedure ([Wang et al., 2019](#bib.bib33); [Xia et al.,
2025](#bib.bib34); [Ye et al., 2026](#bib.bib31)).

In video generation, feedback first supports refinement of the current
output ([Huang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib9); [Long et al.,
2025](#bib.bib10)). Cross-project methods preserve its benefits by
updating reusable production procedures ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib5);
[Wei et al., 2026](#bib.bib2); [Liu et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)). However,
production-only updates cannot repair failures caused by an unchanged
collaboration policy. They can improve execution of the same
misunderstood objective. LIT uses interaction and production evidence
together to revise the director’s behavior across projects. Its
meta-engineer also learns from the outcomes of these revisions, allowing
the improvement strategy to adapt as the director’s weaknesses change.

#### A.6.1 Preliminaries

Let $`\theta`$ denote an agent’s editable configuration and $`\mu`$ a
distribution over tasks $`x`$. The configuration induces an execution
policy $`\pi_{\theta}`$ over trajectories $`\tau`$. For a task-level
score $`R`$, expected performance is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
J(\theta,\mu)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mu,\;\tau\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)}\bigl[R(\tau,x)\bigr].
``` |  | (4) |

Prompt and agent-program optimization search over $`\theta`$ using
observed performance ([Khattab et al., 2024](#bib.bib25); [Agrawal et
al., 2026](#bib.bib45); [Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib14)). This search
can operate on external resources while the underlying model weights
remain fixed.

Let $`\mathcal{T}_{k}`$ contain the trajectories and feedback collected
at iteration $`k`$. An update procedure $`\mathcal{U}`$ with
configuration $`\omega_{k}`$ produces

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\theta_{k+1}=\mathcal{U}_{\omega_{k}}(\theta_{k},\mathcal{T}_{k}),\qquad\mathcal{T}_{k}\sim\operatorname{Rollout}(\pi_{\theta_{k}},\mu_{k}).
``` |  | (5) |

Adaptive curricula change $`\mu_{k}`$, thereby changing which weaknesses
become observable ([Wang et al., 2019](#bib.bib33); [Wang et al.,
2023](#bib.bib15); [Xia et al., 2025](#bib.bib34)). Meta-level
adaptation can also revise the strategy that constructs improved
configurations ([Ye et al., 2026](#bib.bib31); [Wei et al.,
2026](#bib.bib2)). In LIT, $`\theta_{k}`$ includes the director’s
interaction and production policies, while $`\omega_{k}`$ specifies the
meta-engineer’s improvement strategy. Meta co-evolution makes both
quantities editable. Adaptation of $`\mu_{k}`$ supplies learning
opportunities for this coupled process.

#### A.6.2 Curiosity-driven Proactive Evolution

Proactive improvement depends on finding informative experience beyond
the tasks already encountered. Intrinsic-motivation methods use
prediction-based novelty to guide exploration when external rewards
provide little direction ([Pathak et al., 2017](#bib.bib32); [Burda et
al., 2019](#bib.bib41)). Adaptive curricula move this choice from
individual states to whole tasks, matching new challenges to the
learner’s current capabilities ([Wang et al., 2019](#bib.bib33); [Wang
et al., 2023](#bib.bib15); [Xia et al., 2025](#bib.bib34)). The
resulting progression changes what the agent practices, as well as how
it learns from each attempt.

Video search largely explores alternative realizations of an existing
request. VISTA revises generation prompts, while Co-Director searches
creative configurations before local refinement ([Long et al.,
2025](#bib.bib10); [Song et al., 2026](#bib.bib11)). Persistent
improvement can then use completed productions to identify recurring
weaknesses ([Wei et al., 2026](#bib.bib2); [Liu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib3)). Reactive improvement cannot address a weakness that
existing tasks never expose or the evaluator fails to recognize.
Repeatedly optimizing the same observed defects can therefore leave
entire capabilities unexplored. LIT’s meta-engineer examines external
productions and technical analyses to identify untested capabilities and
neglected evaluation criteria. It probes candidate improvements through
directed experiments, allowing evolution to investigate problems absent
from the existing failure record.

#### A.6.3 Meta Co-Evolution

Meta co-evolution concerns the coupling between an improving system and
its improvement mechanism. Agent-design methods search over candidate
systems using execution feedback ([Hu et al., 2025](#bib.bib26); [Zhang
et al., 2025b](#bib.bib27); [Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib14)). Adaptive
curricula expand this search by changing the challenges presented to the
learner ([Wang et al., 2019](#bib.bib33); [Xia et al.,
2025](#bib.bib34)). An additional degree of adaptation arises when the
strategy that constructs improved systems is itself revised ([Ye et al.,
2026](#bib.bib31)). Progress then depends on learning effective
revisions as well as retaining their results.

Within video production, VideoWeaver evolves composition skills and the
creator skills used to construct them ([Wei et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)).
CineForge instead formalizes how recurrent defects become validated
production-policy updates ([Liu et al., 2026](#bib.bib3)). Updating
production resources does not by itself improve the optimizer’s
diagnosis and revision strategy. A fixed improvement procedure can
retain the same blind spots even as the production system changes. LIT
exposes the meta-engineer’s governing skills to revision alongside the
director’s skills. The consequences of earlier interventions inform
later problem selection and solution development. The improvement
mechanism can therefore adapt its diagnosis and revision strategy as the
production system develops.

## Appendix B Formal Representation of Evolution Process

### B.1 Optimization Target

LIT optimizes directing and interaction quality. Task requirements
define the target risk, whereas the meta engineer’s current evaluation
criteria define the empirical objective available during evolution.

##### Definition.

Let $`\theta\in\Theta`$ denote a director policy specified by prompts,
skills, tools, and workflows. A task $`t=(z,u)`$ comprises the complete
creative intent $`z`$ and user behavior $`u`$. The trajectory
$`\tau=\mathsf{Rollout}(\theta,t;\xi)`$ contains the dialogue,
production trace, and final video. $`\xi`$ collects execution
randomness. The distribution $`P`$ describes the target population of
user commissions. ID and OOD performance are analyzed under their
respective distributions. The analysis applies separately to directing
and interaction quality. We omit the dimension index until needed.

Let $`\ell^{\star}(t,\tau)\in[0,1]`$ denote the true task loss. The
optimization target is the expected risk

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{R}_{P}^{\star}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{t\sim P,\xi}\left[\ell^{\star}(t,\mathsf{Rollout}(\theta,t;\xi))\right],\qquad\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}\mathcal{R}_{P}^{\star}(\theta).
``` |  | (6) |

At epoch $`k`$, the evaluation program $`G_{k}`$ assigns a computable
loss $`\ell_{G_{k}}\in[0,1]`$. For the sampled tasks and executions,

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{k}(\theta;G)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{1}{n_{k}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{k}}\ell_{G}(t_{k,i},\mathsf{Rollout}(\theta,t_{k,i};\xi_{k,i})),`$ |  | (7) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{G}(\theta)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{t\sim P,\xi}\left[\ell_{G}(t,\mathsf{Rollout}(\theta,t;\xi))\right].`$ |  |  |

The empirical risk guides director revisions, while the meta engineer
updates the evaluation criteria and the procedures used to measure them.
Final testing estimates
Eq. [6](#A2.E6 "In Definition. ‣ B.1 Optimization Target ‣ Appendix B Formal Representation of Evolution Process ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents")
on held-out tasks using independent criteria.

### B.2 Co-evolution Process

We use the policy–evaluation game of adversarial apprenticeship learning
to describe co-evolution ([Swamy et al., 2021](#bib.bib43)): the meta
engineer searches for evaluations that reveal deficiencies, and the
director changes its behavior accordingly. In LIT, $`D_{k}`$ and
$`U_{k}`$ specify the director and simulated-user policies,
respectively. The meta-policy $`M_{k}`$ governs task selection,
evaluation, and the proposal and selection of revisions.

##### Definition.

Let $`E\in\Theta`$ be a fixed, executable reference director, such as a
historical version. External videos, comments, and technical analyses
inform criterion design. Let $`\mathcal{G}`$ be the admissible
evaluation class, including the zero function. Define

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle L(\theta,G)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathcal{R}_{G}(\theta)-\mathcal{R}_{G}(E),`$ |  | (8) |
|  | $`\displaystyle D(\theta)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sup_{G\in\mathcal{G}}L(\theta,G),\qquad\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}D(\theta)=0.`$ |  |  |

The last equality follows from $`D(E)=0`$ and $`D(\theta)\geq 0`$. The
empirical game is
$`\widehat{L}_{k}(\theta,G)=\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{k}(\theta;G)-\widehat{\mathcal{R}}_{k}(E;G)`$.
Estimating the reference term requires execution evidence on comparable
tasks. Define

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\epsilon_{k}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sup_{G\in\mathcal{G}}\widehat{L}_{k}(\theta_{k},G)-\widehat{L}_{k}(\theta_{k},G_{k}),`$ |  | (9) |
|  | $`\displaystyle e_{k}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sup_{\theta\in\Theta,G\in\mathcal{G}}|\widehat{L}_{k}(\theta,G)-L(\theta,G)|,`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle B_{T}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\left[\sum_{k=1}^{T}\widehat{L}_{k}(\theta_{k},G_{k})-\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}\sum_{k=1}^{T}\widehat{L}_{k}(\theta,G_{k})\right]_{+}.`$ |  |  |

Here $`\epsilon_{k}`$ is the gap between the selected evaluation and the
evaluation in $`\mathcal{G}`$ that reveals the largest discrepancy. The
uniform estimation error $`e_{k}`$ accounts for task sampling, reference
estimation, and scoring, while $`B_{T}`$ is the cumulative regret
relative to the best fixed director. External observations provide
evidence of new defects. Reflection and candidate testing use
computation to identify and assess repairs.

For the delivered version
$`\theta_{\mathrm{out}}\in\{\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{T}\}`$, let
$`s_{T}=D(\theta_{\mathrm{out}})-\min_{k\leq T}D(\theta_{k})`$ be the
selection error, and define

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\eta_{T}=\frac{B_{T}}{T}+\frac{1}{T}\sum_{k=1}^{T}(\epsilon_{k}+2e_{k})+s_{T}.
``` |  | (10) |

### B.3 Capability Upper and Lower Bounds

We prove that LIT has a capability upper bound at least as high as that
of a pipeline whose meta-agent keeps its evaluation criteria fixed
throughout evolution. Its guaranteed minimum performance is also higher
when the gains from correcting evaluation blind spots exceed the
remaining errors.

##### Definition.

Under the same initial resources, environment access, and computation
budget $`b`$, let $`\mathcal{A}_{0}(b)`$ and $`\mathcal{A}_{1}(b)`$ be
the director policies reachable by the baseline and LIT. In the nested
design considered here, LIT retains every baseline path at its original
execution cost.

The baseline optimizes the fixed scoring loss
$`f_{0}(\theta)=\mathcal{R}_{G_{0}}(\theta)`$. For any baseline
tolerance $`\eta_{0}\geq 0`$, define

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{0}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\left\{\theta\in\mathcal{A}_{0}(b):f_{0}(\theta)-\inf_{\vartheta\in\mathcal{A}_{0}(b)}f_{0}(\vartheta)\leq\eta_{0}\right\},`$ |  | (11) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{S}_{1}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\{\theta\in\mathcal{A}_{1}(b):D(\theta)\leq\eta_{T}\},`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle\overline{Q}_{i}`$ | $`\displaystyle=1-\inf_{\theta\in\mathcal{A}_{i}(b)}\mathcal{R}_{P}^{\star}(\theta),\qquad\underline{Q}_{i}=1-\sup_{\theta\in\mathcal{S}_{i}}\mathcal{R}_{P}^{\star}(\theta).`$ |  |  |

Thus, $`\overline{Q}_{i}`$ is the best reachable quality, while
$`\underline{Q}_{i}`$ is the minimum quality among outputs satisfying
the method’s optimization requirement. Assume that the fixed score has
an optimal but low-quality policy:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\theta_{b}\in\arg\min_{\theta\in\mathcal{A}_{0}(b)}f_{0}(\theta),\qquad\mathcal{R}_{P}^{\star}(\theta_{b})-\mathcal{R}_{P}^{\star}(E)\geq\Delta>0.
``` |  | (12) |

Let the representation error of the evolved evaluation class and the
total residual error be

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\delta=\inf_{G\in\mathcal{G}}\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}|\mathcal{R}_{P}^{\star}(\theta)-\mathcal{R}_{G}(\theta)|,\qquad\rho_{T}=2\delta+\eta_{T}.
``` |  | (13) |

##### Proposition.

Under the preceding definitions and assumptions,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\overline{Q}_{1}\geq\overline{Q}_{0},\qquad\underline{Q}_{1}-\underline{Q}_{0}\geq\Delta-\rho_{T}>0\quad\text{if }\rho_{T}<\Delta.
``` |  | (14) |

##### Proof.

Preserving baseline paths gives
$`\mathcal{A}_{0}(b)\subseteq\mathcal{A}_{1}(b)`$. Taking infima of the
true risk proves the upper-bound claim.

For co-evolution,
Eq. [9](#A2.E9 "In Definition. ‣ B.2 Co-evolution Process ‣ Appendix B Formal Representation of Evolution Process ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents")
and the reference policy’s zero game loss give

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\frac{1}{T}\sum_{k=1}^{T}D(\theta_{k})`$ | $`\displaystyle\leq\frac{1}{T}\sum_{k=1}^{T}[\widehat{L}_{k}(\theta_{k},G_{k})+\epsilon_{k}+e_{k}]`$ |  | (15) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\leq\frac{B_{T}}{T}+\frac{1}{T}\sum_{k=1}^{T}(\epsilon_{k}+2e_{k}).`$ |  |  |

Including $`s_{T}`$ yields $`D(\theta_{\mathrm{out}})\leq\eta_{T}`$, so
the delivered policy belongs to $`\mathcal{S}_{1}`$. An evaluation
program arbitrarily close to the infimum in
Eq. [13](#A2.E13 "In Definition. ‣ B.3 Capability Upper and Lower Bounds ‣ Appendix B Formal Representation of Evolution Process ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents")
approximates both the director’s and the reference’s true losses, giving

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{R}_{P}^{\star}(\theta)-\mathcal{R}_{P}^{\star}(E)\leq D(\theta)+2\delta.
``` |  | (16) |

Consequently,
$`\underline{Q}_{1}\geq 1-\mathcal{R}_{P}^{\star}(E)-\rho_{T}`$. Since
$`\theta_{b}`$ minimizes the baseline’s fixed loss,
$`\theta_{b}\in\mathcal{S}_{0}`$ for every $`\eta_{0}\geq 0`$, and
$`\underline{Q}_{0}\leq 1-\mathcal{R}_{P}^{\star}(E)-\Delta`$.
Subtracting proves
Eq. [14](#A2.E14 "In Proposition. ‣ B.3 Capability Upper and Lower Bounds ‣ Appendix B Formal Representation of Evolution Process ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents").
$`\square`$

##### Conclusion.

LIT has a capability upper bound at least as high as that of the
fixed-evaluation baseline because it preserves all baseline evolution
paths. Its capability lower bound also improves with more discriminative
evaluation criteria (provided $`\Delta>\rho_{T}`$). This result
motivates jointly improving evaluation and director behavior: identify
overlooked defects, repair them, and control the errors introduced by
these revisions.

## Appendix C Pipeline Implementation

LIT improves a directing system by changing both how it produces an
artifact and how it recognizes a useful improvement. Within a project,
the User discloses intent through interaction, and the Director turns
that information into a workflow. Across projects, Meta uses the
resulting evidence to revise the workflow and its evaluation criteria.
When the current criteria overlook a quality property, Meta can discover
it through external references and adapt tasks to exercise the methods
developed from that discovery. The Controller connects these two loops
by executing the selected role versions.

The implementation makes a production stage the link between execution
and evolution. Skills determine how the stage runs, while its input and
output provide a boundary at which Meta can investigate and test a
change. Infrastructure supplies these executable units and access to
external knowledge. The Director composes them into a project, and the
User supplies the interaction through which its requirements become
known. The Meta section explains how evidence from this process leads to
changes in each role and in Meta’s own methods.

### C.1 Infrastructure

Role workflows need a common way to invoke capabilities and retain the
artifacts those calls produce. We expose the deployed models through
skills, so a workflow can change its directing method while continuing
to use the same execution interfaces. The skill hierarchy allows
workflows to compose these operations into reusable procedures. To
improve a procedure, Meta can consult the reference database and develop
a revision that the Controller makes available in the next project.

#### C.1.2 Skill Hierarchy

A reusable method must specify both an operation and the context in
which to use it. LIT uses three skill types: atomic skills provide
callable operations, workflow skills determine their dependencies, and
library skills select the applicable method. Meta can therefore change a
procedure at the level where the defect arises and make the revised
procedure available to future projects.

##### Atomic Skill.

An atomic skill defines one reusable decision or operation that a
workflow can invoke, whether the operation is performed through
reasoning, a media tool, or an agent session. For example, treating H3
prompt construction as an atomic skill allows Meta to revise that
procedure independently of the generation call that consumes its output.
Tab. [8](#A3.T8 "Table 8 ‣ Atomic Skill. ‣ C.1.2 Skill Hierarchy ‣ C.1 Infrastructure ‣ Appendix C Pipeline Implementation ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents")
groups further examples by their role in execution and identifies the
optional extensions.

|  |  |
|----|----|
|  Role |  Examples |
|  Production operations |  Image/video generation, frame extraction, transcription, audio separation, clip assembly. |
|  Directing procedures |  Shot planning, H3 prompt construction, reference-asset selection, spatial-anchor instructions. |
|  Runtime operations |  Agent delegation, session continuation, task-result submission. |
|  Optional visual analysis |  DINOv3 features, SAM 3 segmentation, RelateAnything relations, Orient Anything V2 orientation, Depth Anything 3 geometry. |
|  Optional 3D workbench |  Panorama conditioning, SHARP Gaussian reconstruction, depth alignment, splat-to-voxel conversion. |

These stages remain separate operations, so a workflow can use the

##### Workflow Skill.

A workflow skill turns callable operations into a procedure by
specifying what must be available before the next step and how its
result affects the subsequent decision. It can call a smaller workflow
just as a function calls a subroutine. Within the Controller’s outer
workflow, the Director executes its role workflow by delegating to
storyboard and shot-generation workflows. Natural-language branches and
loops allow these calls to respond to the current evidence.

A child receives an upstream artifact and an expected deliverable. Its
parent uses the returned artifact to continue or revisit the responsible
step. For example, a storyboard establishes the references needed for
asset preparation, and those assets condition segment generation. If one
segment fails while its upstream plan remains valid, execution can
re-enter that shot’s procedure. The same input–output boundary lets Meta
test a change without repeating plot development.

##### Library Skill.

A workflow needs to find a suitable procedure before it can reuse it. A
library skill provides this selection rule by mapping an applicable
situation to a skill or resource path. Leaf entries hold the executable
instructions at the granularity needed by the task. Selection proceeds
through the hierarchy, for example from a narrative-production entry to
a genre library and then to the relevant storyboard or sound procedure.
Only the selected instructions need to enter the agent’s context.

The parent directory determines when a leaf method is selected, while
the leaf provides its execution instructions. Incorporating an
improvement therefore requires updating both the instructions and the
routing entry that makes the method available in the appropriate
situations.

|                               |         |
|-------------------------------|---------|
| Reference type                | Records |
| Documents and prompt articles | 355     |
| Skills                        | 21      |
| Workflows                     | 85      |

| Contiguous storyboard scenes  | 263     |
| Manual-feedback records       | 17      |
````
