````math
Table 9: Composition of the local reference database.

#### C.1.3 Mock Web Database

A defect can remain invisible when Meta relies only on its own scores.
The Internet database provides external production knowledge against
which to compare a workflow or its output. We use a mock web database to
emulate the Internet, thereby preventing ground-truth videos for test
cases from leaking. It is stored separately from task cases. Meta first
searches typed records and cached summaries, then reads the original
source to decide whether its method or example applies. Meilisearch
indexes titles and content for this retrieval.²⁹²⁹ 29
[https://github.com/meilisearch/meilisearch](https://github.com/meilisearch/meilisearch).
Tab. [9](#A3.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Library Skill. ‣ C.1.2 Skill Hierarchy ‣ C.1 Infrastructure ‣ Appendix C Pipeline Implementation ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents")
reports the reference inventory.

##### Documents and Blogs.

Documents support the step from an observed problem to an explanation or
candidate technique. Collection queries combine a production problem
with a method or tool, such as multi-shot continuity with reference
conditioning. Meta uses technical papers and model documentation to
understand how a technique works, then consults creator tutorials and
production discussions to determine how to apply it.

Relevant pages retain their source links and associated media so Meta
can return from a search summary to the supporting material. During
evolution, the investigation target determines the query, and the
underlying source determines whether the proposed method fits the
workflow.

##### Multi-media.

Media references make a quality claim testable. Film excerpts provide
examples of established production conventions, while AI-video showcases
and making-of accounts connect a technique to generated footage and its
reported failures. Audience comments help locate events that viewers
found problematic. Collection therefore retains the associated clip or
time interval and the context needed to interpret the observation.

An account of a technique can inform a solution proposal. If the source
also identifies a localized failure, Meta can use the corresponding
media as a candidate test example and label the target property from
what is observable. Keeping machine-generated scores under a separate
source type preserves the distinction between an observation and a
model’s judgment of it.

##### Skills, Storyboards and Code Bases.

Once a candidate technique is identified, Meta needs enough procedural
detail to apply it. Capability-directed searches of repository hosts and
workflow-sharing communities retrieve the relevant skill, workflow, or
source implementation. For example, a camera-control investigation can
retrieve a workflow that implements the required movement.
Screenplay--storyboard pairs provide the corresponding reference for
directing decisions. PROSE scenes are indexed in contiguous order,³⁰³⁰
30
[https://github.com/creDreams/PROSE](https://github.com/creDreams/PROSE).
so a retrieved shot remains connected to the story progression it
serves.

#### C.1.4 Closed-loop Controller

The Controller carries learning decisions into execution. Meta adapts
database cases to the behavior it wants to investigate and assigns the
briefs to User instances. The Controller launches their interactions
with the selected Director, then returns the records to Meta. This
separates the choice of what to learn from the mechanics of running the
project.

Starting from $`D_{0}`$, four evolution epochs produce the Director
versions $`D_{1},\ldots,D_{4}`$. The evaluator is updated after each of
the first three epochs, and each update takes effect in the following
epoch. Thus the four epochs run with $`(D_{0},G_{0})`$,
$`(D_{1},G_{1})`$, $`(D_{2},G_{2})`$, and $`(D_{3},G_{3})`$,
respectively, with $`D_{4}`$ as the final Director. Throughout epoch
$`k+1`$, $`G_{k}`$ evaluates both production results and local Director
revisions. Deferring evaluator changes to the next epoch ensures that
the old and revised Director methods are compared under the same
checking rule.

Meta can develop independent changes at their affected stage boundaries
within an epoch. Each proposal retains the source problem and edited
skill together with its local comparison. The Controller publishes the
selected role bundles for the next epoch, without rerunning the entire
task batch after each edit or imposing an aggregate-score improvement
gate. The retained histories of Director, User, and Meta bundles include
a separate evaluator version within Meta’s method. Shared large assets
remain in global storage, allowing method versions to refer to them
without making another copy.

The fixed-evaluation branch remains executable with its original
workflow and costs, without mandatory additional exploration. This is
the retained set of baseline paths used by the capability-upper-bound
argument in
Sec. [B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Capability Upper and Lower Bounds ‣ Appendix B Formal Representation of Evolution Process ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents").

### C.2 Director Agent

The Director must turn a partially disclosed request into connected
production decisions. The workflow builder plans how to carry out the
project using a storyboard that connects each decision to its expected
output and the later work that depends on it.

#### C.2.1 Workflow Builder

The builder starts from the disclosed request and selects applicable
methods from the skill library. Its default dependency order is plot
development, shot planning, asset preparation, segment generation, and
assembly. Each stage receives the available upstream work and must
return the artifact required by the next stage. The builder also
identifies where a user decision can change that dependency chain.

Interaction can then revise the project at the responsible point. For
example, a clarification that changes a plot event requires
reconsidering its shots, whereas a failed generation under an accepted
shot plan calls for a local prompt, reference, or generation repair. The
persistent directing session retains the earlier work while the builder
decides which dependent decisions to revisit. Thus the workflow evolves
with the disclosed intent without discarding unaffected production.

#### C.2.2 Storyboard Builder

To carry a directing decision through production, the storyboard links
the intended event to the media that realizes it:

$`\displaystyle\text{plot}\longrightarrow\text{shot}\longrightarrow\text{asset}\longleftrightarrow\text{segment}.`$

Each plot node specifies a subject’s action and the resulting scene
change, which one or more shot nodes translate into visible events. The
shots refer to the assets needed for generation, and their resulting
audiovisual takes are stored in segment nodes. Assembly then orders the
accepted segments into the delivery.

These links preserve continuity as production proceeds. Several shots
can share an asset, so changing that asset identifies the segments that
need reconsideration. In the reverse direction, an accepted segment can
supply a reusable observation as an asset for a later shot. For example,
an extracted frame carries an observed appearance or state forward
instead of reconstructing it from text alone. Meta also uses these
dependencies to isolate a local revision. Holding the upstream inputs
fixed allows it to compare the artifacts produced by the old and revised
procedure at the affected boundary.

### C.3 User Agent

#### C.3.1 Persona Faithfulness

The User makes interaction necessary by holding the private script and
persona while the Director receives only the public request. Its task is
to reveal intent as that client would, so a question changes the
Director’s information only through the permitted disclosure behavior.
Invented facts would change the task, whereas inappropriate refusals
would prevent the Director from obtaining information the persona should
disclose. The following skill maintains this distinction when answering
questions and reviewing intermediate work.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### C.3.2 Directing Project Scheduling

##### Task Difficulty Scheduling.

The next project should expose behavior for which Meta needs evidence.
Meta therefore starts from a criterion or recently revised skill and
selects a case that activates it. It adjusts shot and character counts
to set the production complexity, and chooses a persona whose disclosure
behavior creates the intended interaction challenge. Depending on the
evolution stage, the adapted case revisits a known weakness or exercises
a newly available method.

##### Defect and Skill Injection.

Meta embeds the target in the task requirements so that completing the
project calls for the intended behavior. For example, a scene requiring
continuity across shots can depend on a private fact that the Director
must clarify under the persona’s disclosure policy. Meta preserves that
opportunity in the public request and assigns the adapted private case
to the User. The Controller executes the interaction, allowing Meta to
observe whether the target behavior actually occurs.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### C.4 Meta Agent

Meta must decide both what to improve and whether a proposed change
actually helps. Its result evaluation supplies defects visible under the
active criteria. Director revision also searches external references for
improvements those criteria may miss. User revision addresses the
response behavior that determines what the Director can learn, while
self revision changes Meta’s ability to identify and investigate
defects.

#### C.4.1 Local Development and Acceptance

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  Parameter |  Categories |  Consequence |
|  Difficulty $`d`$ |      1: direct deterministic check  2: perceptual decision within one stage  3: context-dependent or cross-stage judgment |  $`8d`$ development and $`4d`$ validation cases |
|  Importance $`h`$ |      1: local optional quality  2: recurring quality requirement  3: task-critical failure |  $`\alpha_{h}=0.10,\ 0.05,\ 0.01`$ |
|  Scope $`s`$ |  Number of distinct affected input–output boundaries whose improvement is claimed |  Separate tests with $`\alpha=\alpha_{h}/s`$ |

Table 10: Design parameters for local development and validation.

\tfn@tablefootnoteprintout

|       |       |     |     |     |
|-------|-------|-----|-----|-----|
| $`u`$ | $`v`$ | 90% | 95% | 99% |
| 0.50  | 0.00  | 10  | 12  | 17  |
| 0.30  | 0.05  | 29  | 37  | 56  |
| 0.15  | 0.05  | 104 | 134 | 208 |

Table 11: Required independent local test cases for 80% power at a
single boundary. Columns vary the confidence level. $`u`$ and $`v`$ are
planning probabilities, not measured results.

Across these routes, Meta compares the old and revised method at the
input–output boundary affected by the proposal. Before editing, Meta
defines the expected outcome and fixes how correctness will be judged.
The sample-construction library described in
Sec. [C.4.5](#A3.SS4.SSS5.Px3 "Construction of Positive and Negative Samples. ‣ C.4.5 Self Revision ‣ C.4 Meta Agent ‣ Appendix C Pipeline Implementation ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents")
supplies the corresponding inputs and counterexamples. Its construction
and labeling rules belong to Meta’s research methods and serve all three
revision routes.

The test budget follows the claim being made. Difficulty determines the
breadth of development examples, importance sets the statistical
confidence required for acceptance, and scope identifies the boundaries
at which improvement is claimed. Meta selects and justifies these
categories before development using
Tab. [10](#A3.T10 "Table 10 ‣ C.4.1 Local Development and Acceptance ‣ C.4 Meta Agent ‣ Appendix C Pipeline Implementation ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents").
This confines repeated experimentation to the affected behavior while
retaining an explicit comparison with the method it would replace.

A candidate needs different evidence for development and acceptance.
Development cases expose the mechanism being repaired, and validation
cases select among the resulting alternatives. Once a candidate is
frozen, source-disjoint held-out cases test whether it improves on the
old method. Including both failures to correct and successful behavior
to preserve makes regressions part of the same comparison. Development
and validation counts set the budget for finding a candidate. The
held-out count is instead chosen to detect the anticipated improvement
with the statistical power specified below.

Before candidate development, Meta defines what constitutes a correct
output for the role and behavior being revised, as detailed below. Both
methods are then judged by this binary rule on independent test sources
drawn from the specified local task distribution. Let $`b`$ count cases
where the old method is wrong and the new method is correct, and let
$`c`$ count cases where a previously correct output becomes incorrect.
Their population probabilities are $`p_{01}`$ and $`p_{10}`$, so

|     |                                                  |     |      |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       A_{\mathrm{new}}-A_{\mathrm{old}}=p_{01}-p_{10}.
       ```                                               |     | (17) |

For $`m=b+c`$, a one-sided exact paired test gives

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
p_{\mathrm{test}}(b,c)=2^{-m}\sum_{r=b}^{m}\binom{m}{r},\qquad p_{\mathrm{test}}(0,0)=1.
``` |  | (18) |

Under no improvement, the conditional probability that the new method
wins a disagreement is at most $`1/2`$. The binomial upper tail
therefore controls a false declaration of improvement at level
$`\alpha`$ when $`p_{\mathrm{test}}\leq\alpha`$.³¹³¹ 31 Exact binomial
testing:
[https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.binomtest.html](https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy/reference/generated/scipy.stats.binomtest.html).
Acceptance therefore concerns the behavior changed at this boundary. It
supplies evidence for incorporating that local method without requiring
the entire pipeline’s aggregate score to improve.

To choose the held-out sample size, let $`u`$ and $`v`$ be anticipated
correction and regression probabilities estimated during development.
For a fixed $`n`$, its detection probability under that planning
alternative is

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{P}_{n}(u,v;\alpha)={}`$ | $`\displaystyle\sum_{b=0}^{n}\sum_{c=0}^{n-b}\mathbf{1}\{p_{\mathrm{test}}(b,c)\leq\alpha\}`$ |  | (19) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\times\frac{n!}{b!\,c!\,(n-b-c)!}u^{b}v^{c}(1-u-v)^{n-b-c},`$ |  |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle n_{\mathrm{test}}={}`$ | $`\displaystyle\min\{n:\mathcal{P}_{n}(u,v;\alpha)\geq 0.80\}.`$ |  |  |

The sample size gives at least an 80% probability of detecting the
improvement anticipated from the pilot estimates, using a test at
confidence level $`1-\alpha`$. It is fixed before inspecting any
held-out outcomes, which alone determine the final acceptance decision.

For a perceptual repair of recurring importance at one boundary,
$`d=2`$, $`h=2`$, and $`s=1`$ allocate 16 development cases and 8
validation cases. If the pilot suggests correction probability
$`u=0.30`$ and regression probability $`v=0.05`$, the held-out
comparison uses 37 cases for at least 80% power at $`\alpha=0.05`$.
These are inputs to the affected stage, such as shot descriptions or
short clips, rather than complete productions. Smaller anticipated
effects require more cases, as shown in
Tab. [11](#A3.T11 "Table 11 ‣ C.4.1 Local Development and Acceptance ‣ C.4 Meta Agent ‣ Appendix C Pipeline Implementation ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents").

On that fixed test, eight corrections and one regression give
$`p_{\mathrm{test}}=10/512\approx 0.0195`$, supporting acceptance. Five
corrections with no regressions also satisfy the 95% confidence
criterion, regardless of the additional ties. If the candidate fails the
held-out comparison, Meta returns it to development and uses fresh
held-out evidence for its next assessment. The confidence statement
belongs to each prespecified local comparison, with the scope adjustment
in
Tab. [10](#A3.T10 "Table 10 ‣ C.4.1 Local Development and Acceptance ‣ C.4 Meta Agent ‣ Appendix C Pipeline Implementation ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents").

#### C.4.2 Result Evaluation

##### Initial Evaluation Criteria.

The initial criteria give Meta a starting objective for identifying
production defects, as formalized in
Sec. [B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Optimization Target ‣ Appendix B Formal Representation of Evolution Process ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents").
Each judgment relates an observed result to the applicable requirement
and retains the evidence needed to investigate a discrepancy. This
evidence lets Meta revisit a judgment when it revises either the
criterion or the checking procedure.

Before applying a check, the evaluator reconstructs the production
timeline from media metadata and detected shots. It aligns the
full-audio transcript with an overview grid sampled every 2 seconds and
a grid of shot-first frames, then consults the dialogue and execution
records to locate the relevant production decision.

For example, to investigate whether a generated shot realizes its
disclosed plan, the evaluator compares three frames from the shot with
that plan. If the discrepancy concerns its transition to the adjacent
shot, the cut-continuity procedure inspects 1.5 seconds on either side
of the cut at 4 fps. A suspected discrepancy in the shot’s soundtrack is
examined with the audio-understanding tool. These observations localize
the failure so that Meta can trace it to the responsible decision.

Attribution then requires establishing what the Director understood when
making that decision. The evaluator forks the frozen production session,
asks it to summarize the intended result from the information it
received, and compares the summary with the private specification. The
timeline establishes whether the relevant information arrived before the
decision, while execution records establish whether it was used. For
example, a reference-dependent failure requires checking whether the
reference was actually passed to generation. The resulting assessment
links the observed defect to the earliest failure supported by the
trace.

#### C.4.3 Director Revision

Director revision changes the method that turns a disclosed requirement
into a production artifact. A revision can begin with an evaluated
failure or an externally discovered technique. In either case, Meta must
identify the production decision to change before comparing the
candidate with the current method under the epoch’s active evaluator.

##### Reactive Defect Attribution.

Starting from a reported defect, Meta traces the artifact backward
through the inputs available to each producing step. The relevant
failure is the first point where available requirements cease to be
reflected in the output. Distinguishing a fact never disclosed from one
received but ignored determines whether the repair belongs to
interaction or production. The local test in the following skill then
checks the proposed explanation with upstream inputs held fixed before
the repair is generalized to the workflow builder.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

##### Proactive Defect and Skill Exploration.

To discover improvements beyond the evaluator’s coverage, Meta selects a
production function and compares its method with one to three external
sources. It then constructs a stage-level input on which the reference
behavior or alternative technique would make an observable difference.
Executing the current method on that input reveals whether the proposed
difference identifies a defect to repair or a promising method to
develop. The resulting candidate joins the same proposal process as a
reactively diagnosed failure.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

##### Solution Proposal and Validation.

Meta turns a diagnosed failure into a proposal by identifying the
responsible decision and retrieving a solution that can act there. The
proposal specifies which instruction or operation will change and what
different output that change should produce. Testing alternatives on the
same upstream inputs lets Meta compare that expected effect rather than
unrelated differences between projects.

For this route, correctness means satisfying the target production
requirement under the active checking rule. The comparison is performed
at the boundary where the proposed change is expected to affect the
output. For example, a shot repair is tested on the generated shot,
extending the comparison to assembly only when the claimed effect
depends on assembly. The shared development budgets and paired
acceptance rule above apply at that selected boundary.

An accepted task-specific repair must then become a method the builder
can reuse. Meta first modifies the executable task workflow and
transfers the general rule to its creator and library entry. The
following skill uses validation accuracy to choose the candidate,
resolving ties by tool cost and then edit size. It merges overlapping
rules through pair-wise-skill-merge and repeats testing if the transfer
changes the tested behavior. In this way, local evidence determines both
the adopted repair and the conditions under which future projects should
select it.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### C.4.4 User Revision

A User method shapes the evidence available to the Director. Its
revision therefore aims to preserve the assigned client’s behavior while
making that behavior more faithful to the private task. The comparison
operates on a reply to a fixed conversation, rather than on a generated
video.

##### Dialogue Analysis.

Meta starts from the Director’s actual question and asks how this
persona should respond under the private script. This determines whether
a missing answer was a faithful refusal or a response defect. A correct
reply must satisfy the expected response specification in both the facts
it discloses and the behavior it adopts.

A dialogue fixture fixes the conversation prefix and the Director
message, so old and revised User instructions face the same request.
Contrasting fixtures change the question or persona while retaining the
underlying fact. For example, the same private fact may require an
answer under one disclosure policy and a refusal under another. The
comparison therefore tests fidelity to the assigned persona rather than
rewarding additional disclosure.

##### Persona Faithfulness Enhancement.

The diagnosed response defect identifies the instruction to revise in
simulated-user. Meta develops that instruction on the contrasting
contexts, then applies the shared local comparison to held-out contexts.
The fixed response specification supplies the correctness label. The
skill below makes the accepted change reusable while preserving the
private script and persona as the authority for each reply.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### C.4.5 Self Revision

Meta’s own evaluation determines which defects receive attention. Self
revision therefore investigates whether a score reflects actual quality
or a weakness in the check, and whether external examples reveal a
property absent from the criteria. The resulting distinction is tested
on labeled samples before it guides Director development. The
sample-construction methods developed for this purpose also provide the
labeled examples and stage-level fixtures used across revision routes.

##### Evaluation History Analysis.

Meta examines the scores of cases to which a criterion applies,
scheduling targeted tasks if too few such cases are available. Scores
concentrated at an endpoint or showing little variation motivate further
investigation because they can reflect either a weak check or
consistently good or bad production.

For normalized scores $`s_{i}\in[0,1]`$, define endpoint concentration
$`E`$ and score spread $`V`$ by

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
E=\max\left\{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\mathbf{1}[s_{i}\leq 0.1],\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}\mathbf{1}[s_{i}\geq 0.9]\right\},\qquad V=\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}(s_{i}-\bar{s})^{2}}.
``` |  | (20) |

The audit design uses $`N\geq 16`$ applicable cases and either
$`E\geq 0.9`$ or $`V\leq 0.05`$ to trigger a discriminating sample test.
Labeled positive and negative examples then separate measurement failure
from production quality. If defective examples pass, Meta strengthens
the check or adds the missing criterion. If valid examples fail, it
revises the decision rule responsible for those rejections.

If the check distinguishes both classes, production scores determine the
next investment. Persistently low scores direct repair toward the
Director. Persistently high scores support treating the property as
mastered on the observed tasks and developing a cheaper checking
procedure. The thresholds thus allocate investigation, while the sample
comparison determines which method should change.

##### Criteria Exploration.

History can expose a weak existing check, but an omitted property
requires another source of evidence. Meta searches external production
references for defects and assessment methods relevant to the task, then
compares them with the coverage of its criteria. For a supported gap, it
defines applicability and the distinction between a passing and failing
example before developing the inspection procedure. The following skill
connects that discovery to labeled examples and the shared local
development loop.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

##### Construction of Positive and Negative Samples.

To distinguish a better check from a more permissive one, Meta needs
examples whose target property is established independently of the
candidate check. The construction library maps that property to an
extraction or transformation method.
Tab. [12](#A3.T12 "Table 12 ‣ Construction of Positive and Negative Samples. ‣ C.4.5 Self Revision ‣ C.4 Meta Agent ‣ Appendix C Pipeline Implementation ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents")
gives six worked construction examples, specifying the reference and
contrasting cases for each target boundary.

Each revision route uses these constructions to hold its test inputs
fixed. An evaluator revision is compared on the same artifacts, so the
observed difference concerns classification. A Director revision instead
receives the same stage inputs, allowing Meta to compare the behavior
produced by the two workflows. For User revisions, dialogue fixtures
provide the fixed request against which each reply is judged. The
construction methods are shared, but the required output follows from
the role being improved.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  Target boundary |  Positive/reference construction |  Negative or contrasting construction |
|  Plot to shot plan |  Extract a contiguous screenplay–storyboard sequence. Annotate the event each shot makes visible. |  Remove the shot needed to establish a specified event, or change its depicted action so that it fails the fixed event requirement. |
|  Reference selection |  Build a shot fixture with the required subject and scene references. Annotate which generation input must use each. |  Omit or replace the required reference in the generation arguments. Retain the rest of the fixture. |
|  Character or scene continuity |  Extract adjacent shots with consistent identity and spatial relations. Annotate the relation being tested. |  Regenerate a short shot with an omitted scene reference or an altered character/layout reference. Label the observed violation. |
|  Audio synchronization |  Extract a clip with aligned speech and image. Record the aligned interval. |  Separate the voice from background audio, shift the voice, and remix it with the unchanged background. |
|  Sound continuity |  Extract a continuous scene with a coherent soundscape across its cuts. |  Join shots with independently generated background tracks to create a localized soundscape discontinuity. |
|  User response |  Derive the permitted answer and response behavior from a private script, persona, and fixed conversation prefix. |  Change the question or disclosure condition to require a different response. Retain the underlying fact to isolate the behavioral distinction. |

Table 12: Examples of positive and contrasting samples for local
development.

\tfn@tablefootnoteprintout

The annotation skill records the property and applicability condition,
then establishes its label from the relevant evidence. A media label
belongs to a specified interval or relation, not to the entire film.
When a construction changes the source, its record retains the
transformation and the resulting observation. A generated counterexample
is labeled from what actually appears, since the intended perturbation
may fail to produce a defect.

Augmentation either varies content irrelevant to the judgment or
deliberately changes the target property. This creates useful contrasts
for development, but variants of one source remain related. Sources are
therefore split into development, validation, and held-out pools before
transformation, and all derived variants stay in their source’s pool.
One held-out source contributes one prespecified comparison to the
independent-case count.

The probability analysis in
Eq. [19](#A3.E19 "In C.4.1 Local Development and Acceptance ‣ C.4 Meta Agent ‣ Appendix C Pipeline Implementation ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents")
assumes correct labels and independent held-out sources representative
of the specified target distribution. That distribution also fixes the
meaning of the accuracy comparison. Balanced positive and negative
sampling measures balanced discrimination. To assess performance on the
deployment mixture, the samples must instead follow that mixture’s class
proportions. These construction choices determine what the shared
acceptance test can establish.

##### Criteria Validation and Refinement.

A criterion revision uses one checking rule as its test boundary.
Correctness means agreement with the sample label, and the old and
revised procedures classify the same examples. A newly introduced
criterion is compared with the preceding behavior, which passed the
previously unchecked property.

An improvement can come from detecting a defect that the old check
missed or from accepting a valid example that it incorrectly rejected.
Conversely, a newly missed defect or false alarm counts as a regression.
Thus $`b`$ and $`c`$ enter
Eq. [18](#A3.E18 "In C.4.1 Local Development and Acceptance ‣ C.4 Meta Agent ‣ Appendix C Pipeline Implementation ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents")
as corrected and newly introduced classification errors. Miss and
false-alarm probabilities are also estimated separately on their
respective classes, so an aggregate improvement retains its
class-specific interpretation.

Once a criterion is reliable, Meta can develop a less expensive way to
apply it while keeping the requirement active. For example, a detailed
frame-by-frame coordinate comparison can become a brief position
continuity inspection during frame sampling. That revision concerns the
cost of obtaining the judgment and is compared at the same criterion
boundary.

These local revisions connect the editable criteria $`G_{k}`$ to the
Director method $`\theta_{k}`$ in
Sec. [B.2](#A2.SS2 "B.2 Co-evolution Process ‣ Appendix B Formal Representation of Evolution Process ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents").
When external examples reveal a defect overlooked by the old evaluation,
Meta develops a criterion that can detect it. This criterion then guides
Director development toward a repair. At each changed boundary, the
paired comparison assesses whether the corrections outweigh newly
introduced errors. The resulting sequence implements the objective in
Sec. [B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Capability Upper and Lower Bounds ‣ Appendix B Formal Representation of Evolution Process ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents")
by using better defect discrimination to guide the Director toward its
attainable capability bound. Publication uses the resulting local
evidence without an aggregate pipeline-score gate.

## Appendix D Dataset Construction

Each case couples a video-creation task with a simulated user: the task
defines the creative context, while the persona determines how the user
expresses intent, answers questions, and delegates production decisions.
This section describes the case schema, construction procedure, and
persona-conditioned interaction examples.

### D.1 Data Structure

Each case separates the director’s public input from the simulated
user’s private context and evaluator-only annotations.
Tab. [13](#A4.T13 "Table 13 ‣ D.1 Data Structure ‣ Appendix D Dataset Construction ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents")
summarizes these fields and their roles in the interaction task.

|  |  |
|----|----|
|  Field (JSON path) |  Content |
| Public input & interaction protocol |  |
|  benchmark_case.reference_materials |  Reference assets and descriptions, when available. |
|  benchmark_case.interaction |  Clarification budget and interaction mode. |
| Private task & persona |  |
|  oracle.script |  Story, characters, shot plan, and audiovisual design. |
|  user_profile.description |  Identity, knowledge, style, preferences, and patience. |
|  user_profile.process_expertise |  Method-level expertise and explicit workflow requirements. |
|  user_profile.disclosure_plan |  What to state, reveal on request, withhold, or leave undecided. |
| Evaluation |  |
|  evaluation_points |  Additional requirements for this case during evaluation. |

Table 13: Public input, private user context, and evaluation records in
a dataset case. The director receives the opening request, references,
and interaction settings. The simulated user’s private context contains
the task, persona, and disclosure rules. Separate fields record
evaluation requirements and construction history. Private fields are not
passed directly to the director.

These fields serve three complementary roles.

##### Public brief and interaction protocol.

The benchmark_case records the initial request, available references,
and interaction settings, including the clarification budget. The
opening request can range from an idea seed to a shot specification.
Reference entries identify assets and their intended content. They are
not counts of distinct source videos.

##### Private task and user context.

The oracle organizes the story, characters, and production design. The
user_profile specifies identity, knowledge boundaries, communication
style, preferences, and material readiness. Its disclosure plan
distinguishes what is volunteered, revealed when asked, withheld, or
unspecified. The director obtains task information through the public
brief and actual user responses, not by reading these private records.

##### Assessment and traceability.

Evaluation points, where present, record case-specific output
requirements. Behavioral test points describe expected interaction
behavior. Provenance and generation records track the source material,
transformations, and review history. These annotations are kept separate
from the director’s input.

##### Two interaction goals.

In *specification recovery*, the director elicits requirements already
known to the user. In *co-development*, the user may need alternatives
before making a decision. The source oracle is a reference, not a hidden
mandatory answer. The intent state distinguishes these goals, so an
unspecified creative choice need not be treated as a missed requirement.

### D.2 Data Sources

The 240-case collection comprises 178 FilmBench-derived cases ([Wang et
al., 2026](#bib.bib16)), 46 MovieChat-1K-derived cases ([Song et al.,
2024](#bib.bib17)), four cases from supplied plot material, and 12
authored OOD cases. Source descriptions are organized into story and
production fields, then paired with personas and disclosure policies.
The MovieChat-derived cases include 46 local source clips, ranging from
30.16 to 119.66 seconds (mean: 67.8 seconds). These durations describe
source material, not generated outputs or target durations for the full
collection.

### D.3 Construction and Verification

As shown in
Fig. [3](#S2.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 2.1 Director-User Interaction Dataset ‣ 2 Method ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents"),
construction first organizes the source into a script and design, then
assigns a persona and an initial disclosure state. The opening request
must agree with both the task and the persona’s knowledge: a user can
specify a desired result without knowing how to produce it.

The persona-consistent verification loop uses ordinary clarification
questions and adversarial probes, including false premises and requests
for protected annotations. Reviewers check factual consistency,
recoverability within the question budget, persona fidelity, and
disclosure boundaries. Feedback guides revision of the profile and
disclosure policy. This is an interaction-level check, not a test of
video-generation feasibility. The export records passing reviews for 228
cases and no such review for the 12 authored OOD cases. These records
apply to the reviewed versions. Later edits require renewed validation.
Construction probes are not held-out robustness tests.

### D.4 Data Distribution

The dataset contains 240 tasks, 284 reference-material entries, and 892
planned shots. Initial development, evaluator development, evolution
epochs 1–4, and test each contain 32 cases. OOD contains 16. The OOD
cases comprise ten outlines and six idea seeds. This is a task-level
partition: source-video identifiers can recur across splits.

|                 |           |                  |       |
|-----------------|-----------|------------------|-------|
| Intent maturity | Tasks     | Reference assets | Tasks |
| Idea seed       | 17        | None             | 22    |
| Story outline   | 147       | One              | 168   |
| Supplied script | 67        | Two              | 39    |
| Specified shots | 9         | Three or more    | 11    |
| Total           | 240       | Total            | 240   |

Table 14: Distributions of intent maturity and reference availability
across 240 tasks.

The collection is diverse but not uniformly balanced
(Tab. [14](#A4.T14 "Table 14 ‣ D.4 Data Distribution ‣ Appendix D Dataset Construction ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents")).
Four-shot plans account for 162 tasks. The professional_user flag is
true for 11 profiles and false for 229. It marks explicit method-aware
behavior and does not classify users solely by occupation. Planned shots
describe the task specification, not detected shots or measured video
duration.

### D.5 Persona Settings and Response Examples

Personas vary along identity, production knowledge, communication style,
preferences, and patience. We distinguish *intent maturity* (how
developed the request is) from *process expertise* (which production
decisions the user can specify). A non-professional user may have a
complete story but delegate the workflow. A professional user may
specify a method while leaving other choices to the director. Both must
acknowledge unknowns and avoid inventing new requirements.
Fig. [8](#A4.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ D.5 Persona Settings and Response Examples ‣ Appendix D Dataset Construction ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents")
illustrates this distinction using a shared creative brief and the same
director question.

Shared task. Create a short dialogue scene: preserve the supplied lines,
assign them to the correct characters, and keep speech and on-screen
performance synchronized. The director asks the same production question
of two users with different knowledge boundaries.

delegates implementation. The second adds a supported workflow
constraint. The director should select the method in the first case and
````
