````math
## Appendix E Evaluation Protocol

We evaluate production quality, interaction and intent alignment, and
the evolution of working methods. The first two evaluations comprise the
four dimensions in
Sec. [3.1.1](#S3.SS1.SSS1 "3.1.1 Metrics ‣ 3.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents"):
Consistency, Dynamic, Interaction, and Intent. They contain six reported
aspects and twenty scoring items. Process analysis examines which
methods the agents can use and whether they use them during production.

Consistency is divided into two aspects: visual aspect evaluates scene
layout, character appearance, and blocking, while audio aspect assesses
voice, sound effects, and audio-visual consistency.

Dynamic is evaluated at different granularities. Fine-grained motion
includes physical plausibility and motion coherence. Coarse-grained plot
includes plot coherence and storyboard design quality.

Interaction evaluates director’s timely access to necessary information,
question necessity, adoption of obtained information, question timing,
and feedback provision.

Intent measures alignment between director system and user
understanding, expected output achievement, known requirement
achievement, reference fidelity, and case-specific scoring items.

Each scoring item is graded on a three-level scale: 0 (non-compliant),
0.5 (flawed), and 1 (compliant). Case-specific scoring evaluates the
checkpoints attached to each project in the test set. The score is
computed as the proportion of satisfied checkpoints, with a maximum
total of 3 points. Each dimension’s score is ultimately scaled to 100.

##### Privileged user and evaluator.

For test-time interaction, the privileged User receives the complete
task specification, a user persona, and rules for when to reveal
information. It starts with the specified initial request and provides
further information during the conversation according to those rules.
Its replies remain consistent with earlier disclosures, correct the
Director’s mistaken assumptions, and leave unspecified creative choices
to the Director. When the User explicitly changes a requirement, the new
requirement applies to subsequent work. The privileged evaluator
receives the complete task, case checkpoints, released references,
dialogue, production records, and delivered media. It determines what
the Director knew when making each production decision. Production
consistency is scored against the script that the Director finalized for
production. Intent scores measure whether the result meets the User’s
complete requirements, including those not disclosed to the Director. We
calibrate the privileged rubric on the evaluator development set and use
the same rubric for all compared methods and evolution epochs. Meta can
change its own evaluation criteria but cannot change this rubric.

##### Evidence and independent judgments.

Each case is evaluated in four independent Qwen3.8-27B sessions with
xhigh reasoning effort. Evaluators receive the same source materials and
score without reading one another’s judgments. The evidence package
contains media metadata, timestamped transcripts, detected shots, an
overview grid sampled every two seconds, and the first, middle, and last
frames of each shot. Evaluators inspect the two seconds before and after
each cut at 0.5-second intervals and sample more densely when a
suspected defect lasts less than this interval. They inspect images
directly and use audio-understanding tools to examine the soundtrack.
Transcripts provide the spoken words and their timing. Every score
deduction must name the scoring item, describe the defect, and cite a
frame, time interval, or execution record. If required evidence cannot
be obtained, the evaluation is marked as failed and must be completed
before its scores enter the reported average.

##### Scoring and aggregation.

Except for case-specific checkpoints, each item receives $`1`$ when its
requirements are met, $`0.5`$ for a minor defect, and $`0`$ for a clear
violation. For items scored by the fraction of successful events, we
convert that fraction $`r`$ into a score using

|     |                                    |     |      |
|-----|------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       q(r)=\begin{cases}1,&r\geq 0.75,\\
       0.5,&0.25\leq r<0.75,\\
       0,&r<0.25.\end{cases}
       ```                                 |     | (21) |

If a production item contains several checks, its score is the lowest
score among the applicable checks. A defect that meets an explicit
zero-score rule receives $`0`$, even if another rule would allow
$`0.5`$. Case-specific checkpoints are scored by the fraction satisfied,
without converting that fraction into the three score levels.

We denote evaluator $`r`$’s score for item $`j`$ on case $`n`$ by
$`s_{nj}^{(r)}`$. We first average the four evaluations of each item. We
then average over all cases and items in aspect $`g`$ and multiply by
100:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\bar{s}_{nj}=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{r=1}^{4}s_{nj}^{(r)},\qquad S_{g}=\frac{100}{N|\mathcal{I}_{g}|}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}_{g}}\bar{s}_{nj}.
``` |  | (22) |

Here $`N`$ is the number of cases, and $`\mathcal{I}_{g}`$ is the set of
items in aspect $`g`$. Visual and Audio each contain three items, Motion
and Plot each contain two, and Interaction and Intent each contain five.
Cases and items within an aspect have equal weight. For the four
dimensions reported in the main text, we use
$`S_{\mathrm{Consistency}}=(S_{\mathrm{Visual}}+S_{\mathrm{Audio}})/2`$
and $`S_{\mathrm{Dynamic}}=(S_{\mathrm{Motion}}+S_{\mathrm{Plot}})/2`$,
with Interaction and Intent unchanged. Scores are reported on a 0–100
scale. Values on a 0–1 scale are these scores divided by 100.
Ground-truth videos without an agent interaction receive only production
scores.

### E.1 Production Quality

#### E.1.1 Visual Consistency

##### Scene consistency.

Scene boundaries are identified from the frozen script. Fixed objects
are compared across adjacent shots and against the scene’s first clear
view.

|  |  |
|----|----|
|  Check |  Evaluation rule |
|  Properties |  The comparison covers fixed-object attributes (presence, color, shape, text, material, count), architecture and furniture layout, spatial relations (left/right, front/back, height, adjacency), and environmental conditions (season, weather, time of day). |
|  Grades |  A scene change absent from the script, a missing scripted transition, a changed major structure or layout, or changes to multiple fixed objects receive $`0`$. A slight change to one minor decoration or texture receives $`0.5`$. Stable scenes and valid transitions receive $`1`$. |
|  Valid changes |  A change in camera position is valid if the objects still occupy consistent locations in the scene. A scene-wide color shift is valid only if several fixed objects change consistently with the same lighting or color-grading adjustment. Content shown on a screen within the scene may change. |
|  Evidence |  The evaluation records which scene each shot belongs to, where scenes change, and which objects were compared across shots. SAM3 helps locate suspected changes. Conflicting detections are resolved by inspecting the source footage. |

##### Character consistency.

Visible people are identified before being matched to scripted
characters. Each character is tracked through occlusions until an
explicit exit or the end of the scene.

|  |  |
|----|----|
|  Check |  Evaluation rule |
|  Appearance |  The comparison covers identity, face, gender presentation, body shape, hairstyle, hair color, clothing, and identifying marks across appearances. Close-ups provide additional evidence from hands, nails, shoes, and accessories. |
|  Identity grades |  A change to a defining character feature, an unexplained change in the number of main characters, or a duplicate main character receives $`0`$. A minor change to an accessory or clothing detail receives $`0.5`$. One unexplained appearance of a background person receives $`0.5`$. Repeated cases receive $`0`$. Entrances and exits explained by the action are accepted. |
|  Style grades |  Each pair of characters is compared in terms of line shape, outline thickness, coloring, detail level, and facial-feature rendering. A noticeable mismatch receives $`0.5`$. A severe difference in style receives $`0`$. Changes in detail visibility caused by shot scale are accepted. |
|  Evidence and score |  Appearance and style are compared using a sheet of character close-ups at least 768 pixels wide. If comparisons between characters’ styles are missing, the style score cannot exceed $`0.5`$. The final character-consistency score is the lower of the appearance and style scores. |

##### Spatial blocking consistency.

The evaluator uses fixed scene landmarks to track where each character
is and how they move. Each interval is described by the number of
characters, their roles, positions, facing directions, postures,
heights, and movements. A new interval starts when one of these changes.
Main characters participate in the central action or composition.
Background people are part of the setting.

|  |  |
|----|----|
|  Check |  Evaluation rule |
|  Counts |  An extra or duplicated main character receives $`0`$, as does a background crowd in a scene that should be empty. Two subjects visibly merging into one, or one splitting into two, also receives $`0`$. |
|  Spatial continuity |  Each main character’s position and orientation are compared before and after a cut or occlusion. A change is accepted if the footage shows the movement, or if fixed landmarks show that the apparent change comes from the camera viewpoint. A change in location or orientation that neither explanation accounts for receives $`0`$. |
|  State changes |  A small position shift that preserves the characters’ spatial relationships receives $`0.5`$. A character changing from sitting to standing without a visible transition receives $`0`$ here and is also checked under motion continuity. |
|  Evidence |  The footage around each suspected change is inspected. Scene anchors establish continuity through occlusion, darkness, reverse shots, and camera moves, rather than screen position alone. The record covers every shot. |

Consistent character counts and positions receive $`1`$. Otherwise, the
lowest score required by the rules above applies.

#### E.1.2 Audio Consistency

##### Voice consistency.

The audio evaluator listens to the full soundtrack and groups spoken
lines by character. It then checks whether each character’s voice
remains consistent across their lines.

|  |  |
|----|----|
|  Check |  Evaluation rule |
|  Voice properties |  The evaluation covers pitch, timbre, accent, speech rate, voice-model switches, abrupt tonal changes, and truncated speech. Switching between different characters is a valid speaker change. |
|  Artifacts and grades |  Unintended overlapping voices, cross-talk, garbled speech, electrical noise, pops, and digital distortion receive $`0`$. A limited voice discontinuity receives $`0.5`$. Stable voices receive $`1`$. |
|  Measurement |  ASR supplies spoken words, and metadata supplies duration. Listening provides evidence of timbre and audible edits. Voices are separated when needed to compare one character’s lines. The mean cosine similarity between that character’s voiceprints provides an additional measure: a value $`\geq 0.85`$ supports a consistent voice, while $`<0.65`$ supports an inconsistent voice. Listening resolves conflicting evidence. |
|  Missing audio |  A video without an audio stream receives $`0`$. The evaluation retains the audio analysis and the timestamp of each defect. |

##### Soundtrack consistency.

Music continuity and audible editing defects are scored separately. The
lower score is the soundtrack-consistency score.

|  |  |
|----|----|
|  Check |  Evaluation rule |
|  Music |  Music segments are compared in terms of instrumentation, rhythm, and emotional character. Smooth, narratively motivated changes are accepted. Abrupt starts, cuts, and stylistic breaks are defects even at scene changes. |
|  Splices |  The soundtrack is inspected for audible edits, distortion, unnatural gaps, and discontinuities at segment boundaries. |
|  Grades |  Both checks use the full soundtrack from the voice-consistency evaluation. Each receives $`1`$ for coherent sound, $`0.5`$ for a localized defect, and $`0`$ for a disruptive break or distortion. |
|  Missing audio |  A missing audio stream receives $`0`$. Audio-visual timing is scored separately under audio-visual synchronization. |

##### Audio-visual synchronization.

The production script distinguishes on-screen dialogue, off-screen
dialogue, and narration. Inspection covers every interval in which
speech is detected or a visible character appears to be speaking.
Character identities are tracked across frontal views, profiles, and
mirror reflections. Each on-screen dialogue segment is checked for:

|  |  |
|----|----|
|  Check |  Evaluation rule |
|  Wrong speaker |  The active-speaker detector consistently identifies a different character as more likely to be speaking than the scripted speaker. |
|  Static mouth |  During at least one second of speech, the speaker’s mouth opening changes by less than $`2\%`$ of face height. |
|  Silent mouth motion |  A character’s mouth moves as if speaking for at least one second, but the scripted on-screen line is inaudible. |
|  Timing offset |  In at least two of three overlapping SyncNet windows, audio leads video, or video leads audio, by more than three frames. The direction of the offset must agree in both windows. |

Active-speaker detection uses TalkNet,³²³² 32
[https://github.com/TaoRuijie/TalkNet](https://github.com/TaoRuijie/TalkNet).
and temporal alignment uses SyncNet.³³³³ 33
[https://www.robots.ox.ac.uk/~vgg/software/lipsync/](https://www.robots.ox.ac.uk/~vgg/software/lipsync/).
The evaluation checks speaker identity, reflections, mouth state, and
timing, and records detector coverage for each speech interval. If a
face track covers only part of an interval, only its valid part is used.
Lip synchronization is assessed for on-screen speech. One failed
dialogue segment receives $`0.5`$, two or more receive $`0`$, and a
video in which all applicable segments pass receives $`1`$. An
audio/video duration mismatch of at least three seconds caps the
synchronization score at $`0.5`$. A missing audio stream receives $`0`$.

#### E.1.3 Motion Quality

##### Physical plausibility.

Continuous footage is inspected for physically implausible changes in
characters, objects, and their interactions.

|  |  |
|----|----|
|  Check |  Evaluation rule |
|  Properties |  The evaluation checks whether bodies or objects pass through each other, float without support, violate gravity, or make implausible contact. It also covers deformed limbs, objects, or faces, flicker, frozen or solid-color frames, and disappearing foreground objects or body parts. |
|  Zero-score violations |  A score of $`0`$ applies to clear interpenetration or deformation, an object appearing or disappearing without moving into or out of view, or a blurred region becoming a new object or character without explanation. A score of $`0`$ also applies if an object’s outline crosses through a solid surface for at least two frames. |
|  Severity grades |  A score of $`0`$ applies if a main subject persistently merges with another object, deforms, or makes physically incorrect contact. Otherwise, one localized defect receives $`0.5`$, and a severe defect or at least two moderate defects receive $`0`$. A video with no confirmed physical defect receives $`1`$. |
|  Evidence |  Suspected anomalies are re-examined at intervals of 0.5 seconds or less to rule out occlusion, mistaken identity, or cuts. The record includes each defect’s type, timestamp, severity, and evidence. |

The lowest score required by these rules applies. Comedic scenes are
evaluated under the same physical plausibility rules.

##### Motion continuity.

For each character, the evaluation records the action and its progress,
posture, height, position relative to fixed landmarks, facing and
movement directions, interaction partners, physical contacts, and held
props. Speed is measured in body heights per second. The character is
compared immediately before and after each cut or occlusion, using 0.5–1
second on either side of each cut and the full action when needed.

|  |  |
|----|----|
|  Check |  Evaluation rule |
|  Action phases |  A score of $`0`$ applies if part of an action is skipped, repeated, or reversed, or if a character changes state without the intervening movement. Examples include standing up, stopping a walk, or recovering from a fall without showing the transition. |
|  Direction |  A change in movement direction exceeding $`90^{\circ}`$ without a visible turn receives $`0`$. |
|  Cross-cut speed |  For an action that continues across a cut, the speed ratio is the larger of the two median speeds on either side divided by the smaller. A ratio of 1.5–2.5 receives $`0.5`$. A ratio above 2.5 receives $`0`$. An abrupt stop followed by rapid resumption receives $`0`$. |
|  Freezing and slowdown |  When the script requires normal-speed action, the score is $`0`$ for a freeze or near-still slow motion lasting at least 0.5 seconds. The score is also $`0`$ if speed drops below half the speed in the adjacent action intervals. |
|  Action duration |  A normal-speed fall, roll, strike, or dodge taking more than two seconds receives $`0`$. Running below 0.5 body heights per second for at least two seconds also receives $`0`$. |
|  Other grades |  Limited stiffness or one or two minor discontinuities that do not trigger a zero-score rule receive $`0.5`$. Natural action progression and appropriate speed receive $`1`$. |

Displacement is measured relative to fixed scene landmarks or from
tracked joints, then divided by character height and elapsed time. The
evaluation records each character’s states and the rules used to score
any defects. The lowest applicable score is used.

#### E.1.4 Narrative and Shot Design

##### Plot coherence.

The evaluator uses the video and transcript to reconstruct the sequence
of events, judging only the portion the user requested.

|  |  |
|----|----|
|  Check |  Evaluation rule |
|  Structure |  The evaluation assesses whether the requested portion has a clear setup, development, and resolution, and whether the order of events and their causal connections are understandable. |
|  Pacing |  The evaluation covers pacing, redundant passages, identical repeated footage or dialogue, and an abrupt ending. |
|  Grades |  Coherent progression with suitable pacing receives $`1`$. One or two minor narrative jumps or localized dragging receive $`0.5`$. Missing essential narrative structure, substantial repetition, identical repeated dialogue, or an unmotivated abrupt ending receives $`0`$. |
|  Delivery scope |  A requested local preview is evaluated as a preview. Later story events outside that delivery scope are excluded. |

##### Storyboard design.

Storyboard design is assessed through changes in shot scale,
composition, the narrative purpose of camera choices, and transitions
between shots.

|  |  |
|----|----|
|  Check |  Evaluation rule |
|  Framing |  The evaluation checks whether framing and camera movement direct attention to the intended subject, emotion, and action at the right pace. Shots that repeat the same scale, viewpoint, composition, and story information receive $`0.5`$. Incoherent shot choices or compositions that fail to present the intended subject or action receive $`0`$. |
|  Proportions |  The proportions of at least two identifiable features, such as a face and a doorway, are compared with their references and across shots. Measurements include each feature’s width, height, and aspect ratio. Systematic stretching or compression receives $`0`$. A change in a feature’s aspect ratio above $`15\%`$ receives $`0.5`$. |
|  Jump cuts |  Between similar camera positions and angles, the evaluation checks for abrupt changes in composition, brightness, character state, and scene structure. One flash-like jump cut receives $`0.5`$. Repeated or strong jumps receive $`0`$. |
|  Camera motion |  The evaluation examines how the camera moves between its starting and ending views. An unexplained direction change above $`90^{\circ}`$ or a ratio of higher to lower camera speed above 2.5 receives $`0`$. |

Framing that serves the story and coherent transitions receive $`1`$. A
minor design weakness receives $`0.5`$, and a severe break in the story
or camera movement receives $`0`$. The lowest applicable score is used.
Motion continuity assesses the subject’s movement. Storyboard design
assesses the camera and editing.

### E.2 Interaction and Intent Alignment

#### E.2.1 Interaction Quality

The interaction timeline places questions, replies, user revisions,
production decisions, and previews in order from the initial request
through delivery. Each item is scored from the number of events defined
below and the fraction that meet its requirements. The evaluation
records both counts, the fraction, and the resulting score.

##### Timely information acquisition.

This item covers production decisions that require information missing
from the initial request. A decision counts as successful only if the
Director obtained all of that information before starting the work that
needed it. We denote the number of these decisions by
$`N_{\mathrm{dep}}`$ and the number for which information arrived in
time by $`N_{\mathrm{ready}}`$. The score is

|     |                                                                  |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       s_{\mathrm{acquisition}}=q(N_{\mathrm{ready}}/N_{\mathrm{dep}}).
       ```                                                               |     |

If no decision requires additional information, the
information-acquisition score is $`1`$. The evidence records when the
information was provided and when the work requiring it began. A
question that the User did not answer does not count as obtaining the
information.

##### Question necessity.

The question count excludes greetings, progress notifications, and
delivery notices. A question is necessary when its answer is not already
available and would affect the pending production decision. We denote
the total number of questions by $`N_{q}`$ and the number that are
necessary by $`N_{\mathrm{necessary}}`$. The score is

|     |                                                         |     |
|-----|---------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       s_{\mathrm{necessity}}=q(N_{\mathrm{necessary}}/N_{q}).
       ```                                                      |     |

If there are no questions, the score is $`1`$ when the Director already
had the necessary information and $`0`$ otherwise. Repeating a request
for an already established fact does not count as a necessary question.

##### Information adoption.

Each distinct User constraint is traced through the production decisions
it affects. It counts as adopted only if all those decisions follow it
and subsequent work continues to do so, unless the User changes it.
Production records provide evidence of its use. With $`N_{c}`$
applicable constraints and $`N_{\mathrm{adopted}}`$ adopted constraints,
the score is

|     |                                                      |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       s_{\mathrm{adoption}}=q(N_{\mathrm{adopted}}/N_{c}).
       ```                                                   |     |

The latest version confirmed by the User applies to work performed after
that confirmation. If there are no applicable constraints, the score is
$`1`$ when the available information suffices for production and $`0`$
otherwise. Information adoption measures whether production decisions
use the constraint, whereas disclosed-requirement fulfillment measures
whether the delivered video satisfies it.

##### Question timing.

The necessary questions identified above are scored according to their
timing in the production process:

|  |  |
|----|----|
|  Score |  Timing rule |
|  $`1`$ |  The question was asked before the planning, asset preparation, or generation step that needed the answer, and the answer was used. |
|  $`0.5`$ |  The question was asked earlier than needed, but its answer was later used, or it was asked after the affected work began, while that work could still be corrected at low cost. |
|  $`0`$ |  The answer was never used, or the question was asked only after delivery or after work had to be discarded or redone because the information was missing. |

The mean timing score over necessary questions is converted using $`q`$
in
Eq. [21](#A5.E21 "In Scoring and aggregation. ‣ Appendix E Evaluation Protocol ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents").
If there are no necessary questions, the score is $`1`$ when required
information was available before production and $`0`$ otherwise.
Unnecessary questions are scored under question necessity.

##### Feedback closure.

Each requested preview, stage confirmation, and delivery review counts
as a feedback event. An event is complete when the Director receives the
User’s decision and follows it by continuing, revising, or stopping.
With $`N_{f}`$ feedback events and $`N_{\mathrm{closed}}`$ completed
events, the score is

|     |                                                     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       s_{\mathrm{feedback}}=q(N_{\mathrm{closed}}/N_{f}).
       ```                                                  |     |

The score is $`1`$ if no feedback event is required and production is
completed. A requested preview that has not been provided, or a
requested revision that has not been resolved, counts as incomplete.

#### E.2.2 Intent Fulfillment

##### Intent understanding.

After production, we resume a separate copy of the recorded Creator
session and ask it to summarize the task: what to deliver, what it must
contain, which constraints apply, which creative choices it may make,
and which requirements remain unclear. This copy can use only the
information available in the original session. It receives no private
script, case checkpoint, evaluator conclusion, or reference answer. The
evaluator compares its summary with the User’s complete specification. A
summary that captures the requirements completely without a critical
misunderstanding receives $`1`$. A broadly correct summary that omits a
minor requirement receives $`0.5`$. A critical misunderstanding,
omission, or contradiction receives $`0`$. If the recorded session
cannot be restored, the evaluation uses its pre-production brief and
plans and identifies this evidence source in the result.

##### Full-intent fulfillment.

The final output is evaluated against the User’s complete specification,
including requirements the Director never learned.

|  |  |
|----|----|
|  Check |  Evaluation rule |
|  Specifications |  Duration, resolution, frame rate, and shot count are checked using media metadata and shot records. |
|  Content |  Dialogue, narration, visible elements, scenes, and music style are checked against the video, transcript, and audio observations. |
|  Grades |  A result meeting all requirements receives $`1`$. Minor deviations, such as one or two missing details or a duration discrepancy, receive $`0.5`$. An unmet core requirement, missing core scene, or fundamentally incorrect narration receives $`0`$. |

For each requirement, the evaluation records whether the delivered video
satisfies it and cites the relevant footage or audio.

##### Disclosed-requirement fulfillment.

This item uses the same checks as full-intent fulfillment but covers
only requirements known to the Director when it made the relevant
production decisions.

|  |  |
|----|----|
|  Check |  Evaluation rule |
|  Specifications |  Disclosed numerical specifications are checked against metadata. |
|  Content |  Disclosed speech, visual content, scenes, and sound requirements are checked against the delivered media. |
|  Scope |  A revised requirement applies to work performed after the User communicated it. The evaluation covers only the requested deliverable, which may be a local preview rather than a complete video. |
|  Grades |  The score is $`1`$ if all disclosed requirements are met, $`0.5`$ for minor deviations, and $`0`$ if a critical disclosed requirement is not met. |

Requirements that the Director should have asked about but never learned
are assessed under interaction and full-intent fulfillment.

##### Reference fidelity.

Reference fidelity measures whether the delivered video follows each
reference supplied to the Director for its intended purpose.

|  |  |
|----|----|
|  Check |  Evaluation rule |
|  Characters |  The character’s face, hairstyle, hair color, clothing, accessories, and body shape are compared with the reference. The evaluation cites the frames used for the comparison. |
|  Scenes |  The referenced environment is located in the video and compared using three to five identifying features from its room structure, furniture layout, wall decoration, windows, lighting, and outdoor features. |
|  Audio |  The relevant soundtrack intervals are compared with the reference voice or musical style in terms of timbre, rhythm, and emotional delivery. |

For each reference, the score is $`1`$ if the output follows it, $`0.5`$
for a limited mismatch, and $`0`$ for a missing required reference
subject or substantial mismatch. The lowest score across all references
is used. The score is $`1`$ if no reference material was supplied.

##### Case-specific checkpoints.

Each checkpoint is evaluated using the scoring rule supplied with the
case. Here $`K`$ denotes the number of checkpoints with a scoring rule,
and $`z_{k}`$ equals $`1`$ if checkpoint $`k`$ is satisfied and $`0`$
otherwise. The score is the fraction of checkpoints satisfied:

|     |                                                          |     |      |
|-----|----------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       s_{\mathrm{checkpoints}}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}z_{k}.
       ```                                                       |     | (23) |

Every checkpoint has the same weight, regardless of its priority label.
The resulting fraction is retained without rounding or conversion to
$`0`$, $`0.5`$, or $`1`$. Each checkpoint is recorded as satisfied,
partial, or unsatisfied, with supporting evidence. Partial fulfillment
counts as success only if its stated rule permits it. For each unmet
checkpoint, the evaluation records why it was not satisfied: the
Director lacked the information, failed to implement a known
requirement, the User refused, production did not reach the relevant
stage, or the evidence was insufficient. If a case has no checkpoints
with explicit scoring rules, its score is
$`(s_{\mathrm{understanding}}+2s_{\mathrm{full\text{-}intent}})/3`$.

### E.3 Evolution Process Analysis

We examine the agents’ skills and execution records from each epoch. The
same checklist and counting rules are used for every epoch. We report
technical maturity, user collaboration, and changes to Meta’s evaluation
criteria separately.

#### E.3.1 Technical Maturity

Technical maturity covers the Director’s production methods, its
self-review methods during production, and the directing techniques it
can use. We assess these from the Director’s skills and the materials
they link to. In Director methods and Director reviewing methods, each
item receives $`1`$ if these instructions explain when to use it, how to
carry it out, and what to do with its result. It receives $`0.5`$ if a
step is missing or the instructions conflict, and $`0`$ if the method is
absent or only suggested in a report.

The final Technical Maturity score is the average of the three category
scores:

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
M=\frac{1}{3}\sum_{g=1}^{3}M_{g},\qquad M_{g}=\frac{1}{n_{g}}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{g}}m_{gj}.
``` |  |

Here, $`M`$ is the final score, and $`M_{g}`$ is the score for category
$`g`$. The number of items in each category is $`n_{1}=8`$, $`n_{2}=7`$,
and $`n_{3}=16`$. $`m_{gj}`$ is the score for item $`j`$ in category
$`g`$. Both category and the final score range from $`0`$ to $`1`$.

##### Director methods.

We score the following eight Director methods.

|  |  |
|----|----|
|  Method |  Executable requirement |
|  Clarification and continuation |  The Director identifies missing information and asks the User for it. After a preview or reply, it follows the User’s decision to approve, revise, continue, or stop. |
|  Narrative planning |  The plan translates the request into a sequence of events, specifies the characters’ relationships and the order of actions, and establishes what each shot tells the viewer. |
|  Reusable continuity assets |  Recurring characters, scenes, and props have shared specifications. The workflow covers preparation and selection of their reference assets and reuse in later shots. |
|  State transitions |  The plan specifies how each action or prop change starts, develops, and ends. The next shot continues from the state reached in the preceding shot. |
|  Motivated camera design |  Framing, camera position, eyelines, and cuts are chosen to clarify the scene’s spatial relationships and story. |
|  Stage-level review |  Plans and assets are reviewed before work that uses them begins. The review procedure distinguishes problems requiring a local correction, regeneration, or a question to the User. |
|  Audio planning |  Dialogue, narration, music, and sound effects are planned separately. Required lines are preserved, and the sound is checked against the action on screen. |
|  Executable integration |  The workflow links to the skills needed to run it and specifies each step’s inputs, output checks, and use of the output in subsequent steps. |

##### Director reviewing methods.

We score the following seven methods for checking its plans,
intermediate assets, and generated videos before proceeding or
delivering.

|  |  |
|----|----|
|  Method |  Executable requirement |
|  Scope reconstruction |  Self-review establishes what the User asked to receive, which requirements were disclosed, and which decisions still await the User’s confirmation. |
|  Event understanding |  Self-review tracks how an event starts, develops, and ends, including when a character or object disappears from view and reappears later. |
|  Evidence selection |  Action judgments use consecutive frames, and sound judgments use the original soundtrack. Disagreements between observations are resolved by checking the source media. |
|  Spatial-temporal continuity |  Appearance and scene layout are compared across shots. The review tracks where characters stand, look, and move, and who holds each prop. |
|  Sound and rhythm |  Self-review checks that voices remain consistent, pauses and speaker changes sound natural, and speech conveys the intended emotion. It also checks how music transitions align with the edit. |
|  Shot selection |  Self-review assesses whether camera position, angle, framing, and composition help each cut convey new information, and identifies jarring cuts between nearly identical views. |
|  Severity assessment |  A defect’s severity is judged by its effect on the User’s intent or the viewer’s understanding, with an explanation specific to the task. |

##### Directing technique repertoire.

We score the following sixteen directing techniques. A technique
receives $`1`$ only if the instructions explain when to choose it, how
to run it with the available resources, and how to use its output.
Otherwise it receives $`0`$.

|  |  |
|----|----|
|  Method |  Executable requirement |
|  Panoramic scene reference |  A panoramic reference fixes the scene layout and provides the basis for reference views of individual shots. |
|  3D directing workbench |  Characters, props, and cameras are placed in a 3D scene. Their spatial relationships are previewed, and views are exported as production references. |
|  Multi-panel references |  Panels show different views or action states and are checked for consistency. Individual panels or the panel sheet are then supplied to the shots that use them. |
|  Character views |  Matching front, side, and back views or facial close-ups are prepared, and references are selected to suit each camera angle. |
|  Music retrieval or generation |  Music is retrieved or generated to suit the story. Candidates are auditioned before their placement, transitions, and volume are planned. |
|  Speech-conditioned generation |  Generated speech is checked for the intended character voice and supplied as an audio input to a video generator that supports it. |
|  Dependency graph |  The workflow records dependencies among assets and generation steps, identifies steps that can run in parallel, and updates affected outputs when an earlier input changes. |
|  Continuity self-review |  The review checks character positions, eyelines, props, and action progression within and between shots. Each mismatch is traced to the production stage requiring correction. |
|  Reusable directing modules |  Directing workflows are saved where the builder can find, select, and combine them for later tasks. |
|  Storyboard retrieval |  Shot examples are retrieved by story function, action, setting, or viewpoint and adapted to the task. |
|  Time-resolved prompting |  Prompts specify when actions, state changes, camera movements, and sounds occur in the generator’s supported format. |
|  Structure-conditioned stylization |  Stylization uses depth maps, normal maps, or other supported structural references. The result is checked for preservation of the intended geometry and motion. |
|  Structured shot prompts |  Shared production specifications are translated into each shot’s subject, setting, camera, lighting, and action fields. Contradictions between fields are checked and resolved. |
|  Explicit blocking |  The plan specifies where characters stand, face, look, and move, and how far their actions have progressed. These states remain consistent when the camera changes. |
|  Conditioning-mode selection |  The generation mode is selected to fit the task and receives the first frame, last frame, or reference media it requires. |
|  Asset candidate selection |  Generated candidates are compared for identity, layout, state, style, and suitability for later production steps. The selected asset is reused consistently. |

#### E.3.2 User Collaboration Patterns

We annotate requests for information, requests for feedback, and
creative proposals in Director-to-User messages. Different acts in the
same message are counted separately. Greetings, status updates,
deliveries containing only attachments, and duplicate transmissions are
excluded. The three categories are defined below.

##### Requesting clarification.

A clarification request occurs when the Director asks for information
needed for production, such as a missing fact, constraint, preference,
or a decision between conflicting requirements. The annotation records
the question, the affected decision, the reply, and whether the reply
was subsequently used. Repeated requests count separately. Duplicate
transmissions are excluded.

##### Requesting review.

A review request occurs when the Director presents a plan, asset,
preview, or completed result and asks the User to approve it or request
changes. The annotation records what was presented, the question, the
User’s reply, and what the Director did next. A video attachment alone
counts as delivery, not a review request.

##### Providing ideas.

An idea occurs when the Director proposes a concrete creative direction
or alternative, or explains a creative trade-off for the User to
consider. The annotation records the proposal and whether it is
accepted, revised, or rejected. Asking what the user wants counts as
clarification. Offering a possible solution counts as an idea. If a
message does both, the proposal and question receive separate
annotations.

For each epoch, we report the total number of clarification requests,
review requests, and ideas. Each total is averaged over the four
independent annotations.

#### E.3.3 Changes to Meta’s Evaluation Criteria

We compare Meta’s evaluation criteria before and after each epoch.
Criteria are matched by what they evaluate, even if their names or
locations have changed. Each change is described by what is evaluated,
how it is checked, the finding or test that motivated the change, and
the epoch when it was first used.

##### Criterion addition.

An addition occurs when Meta starts evaluating a quality property that
the previous criteria did not assess separately. Merely splitting an
existing check under several headings does not count. Each addition is
documented with the defects it detects, the tasks it applies to, and
examples showing how it distinguishes satisfactory from defective
results.

##### Criterion refinement.

A refinement occurs when Meta changes when a criterion applies, what
evidence it uses, how it assigns a score, its thresholds, or which
defects it detects. Wording changes that leave judgments unchanged are
excluded. The record describes how the revised check behaves differently
and cites the examples used to validate it.

##### Evaluation-effort allocation.

We track changes to each criterion’s weight, how often it is checked,
its inspection steps, and its place in the review order. For a
simplified check, the record describes which steps changed, how the
revised procedure still checks the same requirement, and the comparison
used to validate it. A requirement that is no longer checked counts as a
removed criterion.

For each epoch transition, we report the total criterion count and the
numbers added, refined, given a different review allocation, and
removed. Criteria whose checking rules and review budgets both change
count in both categories. We compare the changes in Meta’s scores with
those assigned to the Director’s outputs by the fixed privileged
evaluator.

## Appendix F Comparison Methods

We adapt each comparison method to the common video-generation backend
and interactive task interface. During testing, each Director starts
from the public request and receives further information through
dialogue with the privileged User. Its production plan uses only the
information disclosed at that point. The User retains the private task
specification, and the fixed privileged evaluator assesses the delivered
result as described in
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Evaluation Protocol ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents").

Interaction is added at the orchestration layer. ViMax and VideoClaw³⁴³⁴
34 VideoClaw repository:
[https://github.com/HITsz-TMG/VideoClaw](https://github.com/HITsz-TMG/VideoClaw).
expose production workflows that a top-level agent can invoke directly,
so we give that agent the initial interaction instructions and connect
it to the User. VideoWeaver and GenMAC instead run within our initial
Creator–Director framework. The Creator handles dialogue and passes the
disclosed requirements to the Director executing the baseline method.

Production and revision budgets are method-specific. Using the same
number of evolution epochs does not impose the same number of
productions or the same total cost. The GEPA adaptation below, for
example, requires 64 productions per epoch.

### F.1 Without Evolution

#### F.1.1 ViMax

We obtain ViMax from its official repository.³⁵³⁵ 35
[https://github.com/HKUDS/ViMax](https://github.com/HKUDS/ViMax). We
connect its planning workflow to Qwen3.8-27B, Nano-Banana-2-Lite, and
MiniMax-H3. The video adapter uses first-frame or first/last-frame
generation for one or two conditioning images, and Ref2VA for three to
nine images. Direct reference-conditioned rendering uses an 8-second
default clip duration.

For structured planning, the Qwen client disables thinking and defaults
to a 4,096-token completion limit. Trailing commas are removed before
JSON schema validation. Invalid camera-tree outputs are replaced with
independent camera groups derived from the shot descriptions.
Tool-returned text is capped at 8,192 characters to limit context
growth.

User references are passed to each scene’s frame generation alongside
ViMax’s selected assets, and their submission is checked before video
generation. The portrait stage reuses the generated front view in the
side- and back-view slots. Portraits are generated sequentially, while
ordinary rendering allows four concurrent tasks. Selected character
names rejected by the image service are replaced with descriptive
aliases.

The top-level agent receives our initial interaction instructions and
invokes ViMax’s production tools. It asks for missing information and
returns intermediate artifacts for feedback, then revises the affected
plan or resumes rendering in the same project. Reusable instructions
remain fixed across cases.

#### F.1.2 VideoClaw

We obtain VideoClaw from its official repository. We run its production
workflow with Qwen3.8-27B for text and visual reasoning,
Nano-Banana-2-Lite for images, and MiniMax-H3 for video. The Qwen text
client disables thinking and sets a 4,096-token completion limit.
Production uses 480P, 16:9 reference-conditioned generation with
5–15-second clips and up to nine reference images. Web search,
concurrent generation, and automatic expansion of the agreed brief are
disabled.

Uploaded character and scene references take priority over generated
assets and conflicting inferred descriptions. We pass all associated
uploads to reference and video generation and check their use before
continuing. The H3 adapter separates reference-image conditioning from
endpoint-frame conditioning and requires both endpoints when
first/last-frame generation is selected.

Storyboard segments are designed sequentially. Failed segment designs
and reference-image requests are reported as failures rather than
replaced with simplified designs or older images. The existing
duration-safe segmentation fallback is retained, and failed continuity
reviews leave the generated storyboard unchanged.

We give the top-level agent our initial interaction instructions and
connect its stage-level controls to the User. Requested script or
storyboard revisions update the actual production artifacts before
dependent stages are rerun. The skill library remains fixed across
cases.

### F.2 Single-Project Adaptation

#### F.2.1 GenMAC

We adapt GenMAC ([Huang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib9)) from its official
repository.³⁶³⁶ 36
[https://github.com/Karine-Huang/GenMAC](https://github.com/Karine-Huang/GenMAC).
Qwen replaces GPT-4o for multi-agent reasoning, and MiniMax-H3 replaces
VideoCrafter2 for generation. The Director first prepares a per-clip
design containing object identities, attributes, spatial relations, and
six temporally ordered layout states. After initial generation, separate
model calls perform verification, suggest a correction, route it to the
appropriate specialist, and structure the revised plan for execution.
The three correction routes address stable attributes and spatial
relations, motion trajectories, and changing attributes or states.

Our H3 interface implements the revised layout through textual spatial
and temporal instructions rather than GenMAC’s latent bounding-box and
guidance controls. Each case permits an initial generation pass and at
most one targeted regeneration pass, including user-requested rework.
The revised result is verified again before delivery. These changes
define the GenMAC adaptation evaluated with our generation backend.

We use the initial framework, with GenMAC governing the Director’s
design and visual revision procedure. Initial production tools provide
multi-shot assembly and audio handling. GenMAC’s verification uses the
disclosed request and generated frames, while the privileged evaluation
remains outside the revision loop. The method is fixed across cases, and
its corrections apply to the current production.

### F.3 Cross-Project Evolution

#### F.3.1 GEPA

We adapt GEPA ([Agrawal et al., 2026](#bib.bib45)) from its official
repository.³⁷³⁷ 37
[https://github.com/gepa-ai/gepa](https://github.com/gepa-ai/gepa). GEPA
treats the Director’s skill files as optimizable text components. In
each evolution epoch, it draws a fresh set of 32 development cases,
split into 24 training and 8 validation cases. The current skill set is
first evaluated on all 32 cases, producing the execution traces and
feedback used for reflection. Four modify-and-verify iterations follow.
In each iteration, the controller inspects the collected traces and
feedback and selects the single skill most implicated in the
failures—only one skill is revised at a time, as a revision already
propagates through a long chain of dependent production stages—and a
Qwen3.8-27B reflection model proposes the revised text. The revised
candidate is validated on the eight validation cases and accepted only
on strict improvement, entering the Pareto front from which the parent
of the next iteration is selected.

Each iteration costs eight productions, and one epoch costs 64
productions in total, about twice the sample budget of a normal
evolution round. GEPA runs within our initial framework: the Creator
handles dialogue and passes the disclosed requirements to the Director,
whose skills GEPA evolves. The User and the evaluation criteria remain
fixed. GEPA maintains no user model, and its reflection reuses only the
feedback of the current epoch’s cases.

#### F.3.2 VideoWeaver

We obtain VideoWeaver ([Wei et al., 2026](#bib.bib2)) from its official
repository.³⁸³⁸ 38
[https://github.com/JianhuiWei7/VideoWeaver](https://github.com/JianhuiWei7/VideoWeaver).
We use its released skill-optimizer to revise task-specific Director
skills and propagate reusable changes to video-skill-creator. The
optimizer processes each development case using its input, execution
trace, generated artifacts, and evaluation feedback. Within an epoch,
later cases refine the creator already updated by earlier cases. The
resulting creator becomes the starting point for the next epoch. The
User and evaluation criteria remain fixed.

VideoWeaver runs in our initial framework, which has basic interaction
capabilities and corresponding evaluation metrics. VideoWeaver’s
optimizer learns from the resulting records and updates the director’s
production and interaction skills.

- •

- •
  MS (Motion Smoothness) measures whether actions and motion are
  coherent and natural, free of jumps or stuttering.
- •
  DD (Dynamic Degree) measures the amount of motion and change occurring
  in the video, reflecting the model’s ability to “make the scene move”.
  Higher DD is not necessarily better. DD should be interpreted together
  with the consistency and smoothness scores.
- •
  AQ (Aesthetic Quality) measures overall visual appeal in terms of
  composition, color, and lighting.
- •
  IQ (Imaging Quality) measures basic picture quality, including
  sharpness, distortion, and artifacts.

ScriptAgent CriticAgent reports subjective scores assigned by an AI
critic (0–5, higher is better) along five dimensions:

- •
  CCA (Cinematic Camera Articulation) measures the sophistication of
  camera work—shot types, framing transitions, and dynamic movements—in
  supporting the scripted narrative.
- •
  KBL (Kinetic Body Language & Blocking) measures whether character
  motions, physical interactions, and spatial arrangements are specific,
  expressive, and consistent with the scripted actions.
- •
  VDF (Visual Descriptive Fidelity) measures how faithfully visual
  details (character appearance, clothing textures, scene layout,
  lighting) reproduce the descriptive cues in the script.
- •
  EAM (Emotional Arc & Micro-Expressions) measures whether facial
  expressions, subtle gestures, and their temporal evolution reflect the
  emotional progression intended by the script and audio.
- •
  NPT (Narrative Pacing & Timing) measures the alignment of shot timing,
  action beats, and pauses with the narrative structure and rhythm
  implied by the script and audio.

### G.4 Case Study

![Refer to caption](2610.41865v1/fig/initial-storyboard.png)

Figure 10: Production workflow before evolution. Shared text
descriptions of characters and scenes guide timed shot prompts.
Generated clips are retained in full and concatenated, then mixed with
background music. The shown generation calls use no reference images or
videos.

##### Storyboard before and after evolution.

As shown in
Fig. [10](#A7.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ G.4 Case Study ‣ Appendix G Supplementary Experiments ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents"),
the initial pipeline first analyzes each shot, then directly uses the
shot plan and the previous video as conditioning to generate the next
video. Without a global anchor, this easily causes character and scene
drift.

![Refer to caption](2610.41865v1/fig/storyboard.png)

Figure 11: Production workflow after evolution. Shared character, scene,
and prop references guide image preparation for each shot. Generated end
frames provide visual references for later shots. The selection row
distinguishes edited clips (green) from planned edits (orange), which
feed into the final edit timeline.

In
Fig. [11](#A7.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ Storyboard before and after evolution. ‣ G.4 Case Study ‣ Appendix G Supplementary Experiments ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents"),
the story is first expanded into performance beats. Character and scene
references are used to set initial blocking and prepare shot-specific
Cards. For continuous performance, pose, orientation, and prop states
are extracted from the last generated frame as new references. For state
changes, start and end images are used for guidance. When transitioning
to the ball, identity and costume references are retained and the
composition is rebuilt. Finally, footage is selected, trimmed, and
spliced into a complete narrative, coordinating image generation, video
generation, and editing through material dependencies.

##### Failure case analysis.

We show representative failure cases. First, as shown in
Fig. [12](#A7.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ Failure case analysis. ‣ G.4 Case Study ‣ Appendix G Supplementary Experiments ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents"),
when the subjects in the frame are too complex, the video generation
model may find it difficult to ensure consistency, and the VLM may find
it difficult to detect errors. Second, in long videos, there are complex
coupling relationships among the states of multiple subjects. This makes
it difficult for the VLM to ensure the temporal consistency of the
states of some props. Incorporating edge cases during the evolution
process may be effective. Moreover, as foundation models advance, these
problems will also be alleviated.

![Refer to caption](2610.41865v1/failurecases.png)

Figure 12: Representative failure cases. Top: character appearance
changes in a scene with many subjects. Bottom: a stick’s state is
inconsistent with the action sequence. Red boxes highlight the errors.

### G.5 Design of User Study

##### Materials and participants.

The study contains 16 task groups and 48 videos in total. Each group
contains one video from ViMax, one from VideoWeaver, and one from LIT
for the same task. Fifteen participants each assess four groups,
yielding 60 group assessments over this pool of videos.
Fig. [13](#A7.F13 "Figure 13 ‣ Reported comparisons. ‣ G.5 Design of User Study ‣ Appendix G Supplementary Experiments ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents")
illustrates the layout for comparing three videos within a group.

##### Evaluation dimensions and evidence.

Participants rate the videos along Consistency, Dynamic, Interaction,
and Intent, using the dimension definitions in
Sec. [3.1.1](#S3.SS1.SSS1 "3.1.1 Metrics ‣ 3.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents").
They inspect the generated videos and audio to assess Consistency and
Dynamic. For Interaction and Intent, they also read the Agent dialogue
records and the task’s Oracle Script. The Oracle Script provides the
reference requirements, while the dialogue records show what information
the Director requested and received. These materials allow participants
to assess both the interaction process and alignment with the intended
task.

##### Reported comparisons.

Tab. [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ User Study. ‣ 3.2 Comparison between Video Director Agents ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Learning to Interact and Direct: Co-Evolving Video Director Agents")
reports human win counts aggregated over 60 group assessments and
automatic evaluator win counts over the 16 task groups. We report
Kendall’s $`\tau`$ between the human and automatic method rankings for
each dimension.
````
